title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text: Source: R/queries.R

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Description
possible_ancestors() finds every node V that is an ancestor of node in some DAG (for a PDAG-family cg) or MAG (for a PAG cg) in the equivalence class represented by cg. possible_descendants() is the mirror notion in the other direction.

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Usage
possible_ancestors(cg, node, open = getOption("CausalStructures.open", TRUE))

possible_descendants(cg, node, open = getOption("CausalStructures.open", TRUE))

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Arguments



cg


A PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) or PAG graph created with cgraph().




node


Node name.




open


If TRUE (default, from the CausalStructures.open option; see CausalStructures_options), exclude node itself from the result; if FALSE, include it.

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Details
These are the nodes reachable from node by a possibly directed path, one on which no edge is compelled in the direction away from node (traversing an undirected edge, or a directed/circle edge oriented, or possibly orientable, toward node). Both are supersets of ancestors()/descendants(), since those only count edges compelled in the right direction.

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Value
Sorted character vector of node names.

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
References
Perković E, Textor J, Kalisch M, Maathuis MH (2018). “Complete Graphical Characterization and Construction of Adjustment Sets in Markov Equivalence Classes of Ancestral Graphs.” Journal of Machine Learning Research, 18, 1–62.

title: Possible-ancestor/descendant node-set queries
text:
Examples

cpdag <- cgraph(A %---% B, B %---% C, class = "CPDAG")
ancestors(cpdag, "C")
#> character(0)
possible_ancestors(cpdag, "C")
#> [1] "A" "B"
possible_ancestors(cpdag, "C", open = FALSE)
#> [1] "A" "B" "C"

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text: Source: R/data.R

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text:
Description
Simulates observational data from a linear Gaussian structural causal model over cg. Each node is a linear function of its parents plus independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation error_sd, with edge coefficients drawn uniformly from coef_range. If standardize = TRUE (default), each variable is standardized to zero mean and unit variance.

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text:
Usage
simulate_data(
  cg,
  n,
  standardize = TRUE,
  coef_range = c(-1, 1),
  random_sign = FALSE,
  error_sd = 1,
  seed = NULL
)

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG created with cgraph().




n


Number of samples to generate.




standardize


If TRUE (default), standardize each variable to zero mean and unit variance.




coef_range


Length-2 numeric vector giving the range edge coefficients are drawn uniformly from.




random_sign


If TRUE, draw each coefficient’s magnitude from coef_range and its sign independently at random, instead of drawing the signed coefficient from coef_range.




error_sd


Standard deviation of each node’s Gaussian noise term, or a length-2 range each node’s standard deviation is drawn uniformly from.




seed


Optional integer seed for reproducibility.

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text:
Details
A sign-symmetric coefficient range such as c(-1, 1) puts many coefficients near zero, i.e. near-unfaithful edges. To keep every edge’s coefficient away from zero, use a positive range with random_sign = TRUE, e.g. coef_range = c(0.5, 2).

title: Simulate data from a DAG
text:
Value
A data frame with n rows (samples) and one column per node, named and ordered as in nodes().

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text: Source: R/transform.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Description
Applies Meek’s rules R1-R4 to the PDAG-family graph cg until no further orientation is implied, returning the resulting MPDAG.

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Usage
meek_closure(cg, check_cycles = TRUE, r4 = TRUE)

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Arguments



cg


A PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) graph created with cgraph().




check_cycles


If TRUE (default), check every orientation for a directed cycle it would close, and error if a rule implies one: every DAG consistent with cg would contain it, so cg has no consistent DAG extension and no MPDAG closes it. Disabling this can speed up closure when cg is known to admit no such cycle, but then the result is not checked to be acyclic.




r4


If TRUE (default), apply rule R4. Disabling this can speed up closure when cg is known not to need it (e.g. it has no background knowledge beyond the v-structures already encoded in it).

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Details


R1: a --> b --- c, a not adjacent to c implies b --> c.


R2: a --- b, a directed path a --> w --> b exists implies a --> b.


R3: a --- b, two non-adjacent parents c, d of b with a --- c and a --- d implies a --> b.


R4: a --- b, a --- c, and c --> d --> b, with c not adjacent to b and a adjacent to d, implies a --> b.

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Value
A cgraph of class MPDAG.

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
References
Meek C (1995). “Causal inference and causal explanation with background knowledge.” In Proceedings of UAI 1995, 403–410.

title: Apply Meek’s orientation rules
text:
Examples

pdag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %---% C, class = "PDAG")
meek_closure(pdag)
#> MPDAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, B --> C

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text: Source: R/identification.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Description
Returns TRUE if cg1 and cg2 (both DAGs, or both MAGs) belong to the same Markov equivalence class, i.e. they impose the same (conditional-)independence constraints.

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Usage
markov_equivalent(cg1, cg2)

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Arguments



cg1, cg2


Graphs to compare, created with cgraph(). Both must be DAGs, or both must be MAGs.

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Details
For DAGs, this holds iff they share the same skeleton and the same set of v-structures (unshielded colliders a --> b <-- c with a, c non-adjacent) - the Verma-Pearl characterization. For MAGs, this holds iff they map to the same PAG.

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Value
A logical scalar.

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
References
Verma T, Pearl J (1990). “Equivalence and synthesis of causal models.” In Proceedings of UAI 1990.
Ali RA, Richardson TS, Spirtes P (2009). “Markov equivalence for ancestral graphs.” Annals of Statistics, 37(5B), 2808–2837.

title: Test whether two graphs are Markov equivalent
text:
Examples

g1 <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B)
g2 <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B)
g3 <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %-->% C)
markov_equivalent(g1, g2) # same skeleton and v-structures
#> [1] TRUE
markov_equivalent(g1, g3) # different v-structures
#> [1] FALSE

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text:
Description
Lists all sets (up to size max_size) satisfying the Generalized Adjustment Criterion; see is_valid_adjustment(). When minimal = TRUE (default), only inclusion-minimal sets are returned.

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text:
Usage
all_adjustment_sets(
  cg,
  x,
  y,
  minimal = TRUE,
  max_size = 3,
  include = character(),
  restrict = NULL
)

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG, ADMG, PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG), AG-family (AG, MAG), or PAG graph created with cgraph().




x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




minimal


If TRUE (default), return only minimal sets.




max_size


Maximum adjustment set size to consider.




include


Character vector of nodes forced into every set.




restrict


Character vector of candidate nodes sets are drawn from. NULL (default) allows every node except x and y.

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text:
Value
List of character vectors (empty list if none exist).

title: Enumerate all valid adjustment sets
text:
Examples

admg <- cgraph(L %-->% X, X %-->% Y, L %-->% Y, class = "ADMG")
all_adjustment_sets(admg, "X", "Y")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "L"

title: Test d-separation
text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Test d-separation
text:
Description
Two nodes are d-separated given a conditioning set given if every path between them is blocked. A path is blocked if it contains either a non-collider node in given, or a collider node (and all its descendants) not in given.

title: Test d-separation
text:
Usage
d_separated(cg, x, y, given = character())

title: Test d-separation
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) graph created with cgraph().




x, y


Node name, or character vector of node names (to test whether the two sets are separated).




given


Character vector of conditioning node names (may be empty).

title: Test d-separation
text:
Value
TRUE if x and y are d-separated given given.

title: Test d-separation
text:
Examples

chain <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %-->% C)
d_separated(chain, "A", "C") # chain A --> B --> C is open
#> [1] FALSE
d_separated(chain, "A", "C", "B") # conditioning on B
#> [1] TRUE

collider <- cgraph(A %-->% C, B %-->% C)
d_separated(collider, "A", "B") # collider is blocked
#> [1] TRUE
d_separated(collider, "A", "B", "C") # conditioning opens it
#> [1] FALSE

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text: Source: R/construction.R

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Description
Generates a random DAG on n nodes named V1, ..., Vn, sampled uniformly at random from the space of all labelled DAGs on n nodes, using a recursive-enumeration algorithm.

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Usage
uniform_dag(n, seed = NULL, counts = NULL)

uniform_dag_counts(n)

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Arguments



n


Number of nodes. For uniform_dag_counts(), the largest number of nodes the table can be used for.




seed


Optional integer seed for reproducibility.




counts


Optional table from uniform_dag_counts(), computed for at least n nodes.

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Details
Unlike generate_graph(), which samples edges independently (uniform over graphs of a given size/density but not uniform over the space of DAGs), this samples uniformly over the full space of labelled DAGs on n nodes.
Every draw has to compute a table whose cost grows quickly with n. To draw many DAGs, compute it once with uniform_dag_counts() and pass it as counts.

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Value
For uniform_dag(), a cgraph. For uniform_dag_counts(), an external pointer of class uniform_dag_counts to the table, which is held by the compiled library, so it does not survive saving and reloading or a restart of R.

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
References
Kuipers J, Moffa G (2015). “Uniform random generation of large acyclic digraphs.” Statistics and Computing, 25(2), 227–242.

title: Generate a uniformly random DAG
text:
Examples

dag <- uniform_dag(6, seed = 1405)
dag
#> DAG with 6 nodes and 11 edges:
#>   nodes: V1, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6
#>   edges:
#>     V6 --> V5, V2 --> V5, V1 --> V5, V2 --> V6, V1 --> V6, … (6 more)

# Reuse the table across many draws
table <- uniform_dag_counts(20)
dags <- lapply(1:5, function(i) uniform_dag(20, seed = i, counts = table))

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
Description
idp() decides whether P(y | do(x)) is identifiable from a PAG, i.e. in every MAG of its Markov equivalence class, and if so returns it as a formula in terms of the observational distribution, or NULL if it is not identifiable. It implements the IDP algorithm, the PAG analogue of id(). cidp() additionally conditions on given (the CIDP algorithm, the analogue of idc()), reducing to idp() when given is empty.

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
Usage
idp(cg, x, y)

cidp(cg, x, y, given = character())

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
Arguments



cg


A PAG created with cgraph(), without selection bias (undirected edges).




x, y


Intervention (exposure) and outcome node name, or character vector of node names. Must be disjoint from each other (and from given, for cidp()).




given


Character vector of node names to additionally condition on (cidp() only).

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
Value
A character scalar with the rendered formula, or NULL if the effect is not identifiable.

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
References
Jaber A, Ribeiro A, Zhang J, Bareinboim E (2022). “Causal Identification under Markov equivalence: Calculus, Algorithm, and Completeness.” In Koyejo S, Mohamed S, Agarwal A, Belgrave D, Cho K, Oh A (eds.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 35, 3679–3690. doi:10.52202/068431-0266. https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/17a9ab4190289f0e1504bbb98d1d111a-Paper-Conference.pdf.

title: Identify an interventional distribution from a PAG
text:
Examples

mag <- cgraph(B %-->% X, A %<->% X, A %-->% Y, X %-->% Y, class = "MAG")
pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
idp(pag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{A, B} (P(A, B, X, Y) / P(X | A, B))"

cidp(pag, "X", "Y", given = "A")
#> [1] "(Σ_{B} (P(A, B, X, Y) / P(X | A, B))) / P(A)"

title: Compute a graph layout
text: Source: R/layout.R

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
Description
Computes node coordinates for cgraph_plot().

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
Usage
cgraph_layout(
  x,
  method = NULL,
  direction = c("right", "down", "up", "left"),
  seed = 1L,
  ...
)

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
Arguments



x


A graph created with cgraph(), of any class.




method


The layout method. The default (NULL) is "sugiyama" if x has class DAG, and "stress" otherwise.


"sugiyama": layered/hierarchical layout (Sugiyama et al. 1981), from the Sugiyama.jl package.


"stress": stress majorization (Gansner et al. 2005). A good general-purpose choice.


"spring": force-directed layout (Fruchterman and Reingold 1991).


"sfdp": scalable force-directed placement (Hu 2006).


"spectral": spectral layout, from eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian.


"shell": nodes evenly spaced on a circle, in nodes() order.


"squaregrid": nodes on a square grid, row by row in nodes() order.


Every method except "sugiyama" is from NetworkLayout.jl and ignores edge direction.




direction


For "sugiyama", which way the layers flow: "right" (the default), "down", "up" or "left".




seed


For "stress", "spring" and "sfdp", the seed of the random initial positions. The layout is the same for the same seed.




...


Ignored, so that cgraph_plot() can pass its ... through.

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
Value
A data.frame with columns name, x, and y.

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
References
Fruchterman TMJ, Reingold EM (1991). “Graph drawing by force-directed placement.” Software: Practice and Experience, 21(11), 1129–1164. doi:10.1002/spe.4380211102. Gansner ER, Koren Y, North S (2005). “Graph Drawing by Stress Majorization.” In Pach J (ed.), Graph Drawing (GD 2004), volume 3383 of Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 239–250. doi:10.1007/978-3-540-31843-9_25. Hu Y (2006). “Efficient, High-Quality Force-Directed Graph Drawing.” The Mathematica Journal, 10(1), 37–71. Sugiyama K, Tagawa S, Toda M (1981). “Methods for Visual Understanding of Hierarchical System Structures.” IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, 11(2), 109–125. doi:10.1109/TSMC.1981.4308636.

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
See Also
Other plotting: cgraph_grob(), cgraph_plot(), cgraph_plot_grid(), plot-styling, plot_default_options(), plot_options()

title: Compute a graph layout
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %-->% C)
cgraph_layout(dag)
#>   name x y
#> 1    A 0 0
#> 2    B 2 0
#> 3    C 4 0
cgraph_layout(dag, method = "stress")
#>   name           x           y
#> 1    A  0.59924944  0.79995414
#> 2    B  0.02209726 -0.01703984
#> 3    C -0.62134671 -0.78291430

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text: Source: R/plot-options.R

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:
Description
Configure the package-wide defaults for every plot: node_style, edge_style, label_style, and title_style, each a list of the fields taken by style_nodes(), style_edges(), style_labels(), and style_title(). The style verbs still override these defaults for the nodes and edges they select. spacing is the default gap (a grid unit) between plots arranged with cgraph_plot_grid(), | or /.

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:
Usage
plot_options(...)

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:
Arguments



...


Named values to update options with (merged into the existing options via utils::modifyList(), so a partial style list only overrides the fields it mentions), or unnamed option names to retrieve. Multiple unnamed arguments drill down through nested options. Called with no arguments, returns all current plot options. Querying a non-existent option raises an error.

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:
Value
When setting, the previous values for the updated options, invisibly. When getting, the requested options.

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:
See Also
plot-styling for the style fields and per-plot styling, plot_default_options() to inspect or reset to the built-in defaults.
Other plotting: cgraph_grob(), cgraph_layout(), cgraph_plot(), cgraph_plot_grid(), plot-styling, plot_default_options()

title: Get or set global default plot styles
text:

# Query all current plot options
plot_options()

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text: Source: R/identification.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Description
Returns every valid local structure at x in the PAG cg. Each entry is a subset of x’s circle-marked neighbors for which a MAG consistent with cg exists with a bidirected edge to every node in the subset and a directed edge away from x to every other circle-marked neighbor. Pair an entry with maximal_local_mag() to get the corresponding graph; this is the graph-only ingredient pagcauses() enumerates local structures with.

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Usage
possible_local_structures(cg, x)

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Arguments



cg


A PAG created with cgraph().




x


Node name.

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Details
Assumes cg has no selection bias (no undirected edges).

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Value
List of character vectors, one per valid local structure.

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
References
Wang T, Qin T, Zhou Z (2023). “Sound and complete causal identification with latent variables given local background knowledge.” Artificial Intelligence, 322, 103964.
Wang T, Tao L, Qin T, Zhou Z (2025). “Estimating possible causal effects with latent variables via adjustment and novel rule orientation.” Artificial Intelligence, 347, 104387.

title: Enumerate valid local structures at a node of a PAG
text:
Examples

pag <- cgraph(
  X %o->% Y, X %o->% C, X %o->% A, Y %o-o% C, C %o-o% A,
  B %o->% C, B %o->% Y, B %o->% A,
  class = "PAG"
)
possible_local_structures(pag, "X")
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "A"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "C"
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> [1] "A" "C"
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> [1] "Y"
#> 
#> [[6]]
#> [1] "C" "Y"

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text:
Description
Generalizes possible_parent_sets() from a single intervention node to a set xs of simultaneous interventions. Every undirected edge incident to at least one node of xs is jointly reoriented, keeping only orientations that introduce no new v-structure and remain acyclic. Each returned entry is a list of parent sets in the same order as xs (entry i gives a valid parent set for xs[i] under that joint orientation).

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text:
Usage
possible_joint_parent_sets(cg, xs)

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text:
Arguments



cg


A PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) graph created with cgraph().




xs


Character vector of node names (the simultaneous interventions; must be non-empty with no duplicates).

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text:
Value
List of lists of character vectors: one list per valid joint orientation, each containing one parent set per node of xs.

title: Enumerate possible joint parent sets (joint-IDA)
text:
References
Maathuis MH, Kalisch M, Bühlmann P (2009). “Estimating high-dimensional intervention effects from observational data.” The Annals of Statistics, 37(6A), 3133–3164.
Nandy P, Maathuis MH, Richardson TS (2017). “Estimating the effect of joint interventions from observational data in sparse high-dimensional settings.” The Annals of Statistics, 45(2), 647–674.

title: Validate instrumental variables
text:
Description
Tests whether a set of variables are valid instruments for identifying the causal effect of exposure x on outcome y, conditionally on given. Every node in z must be d-/m-separated from y given given in the graph obtained by removing the first edge of every causal path from x to y (exclusion restriction), and at least one node in z must be d-/m-connected to x given given (relevance). given must contain no descendant of x or y.

title: Validate instrumental variables
text:
Usage
is_valid_iv(cg, x, y, z = character(), given = character())

title: Validate instrumental variables
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph().




x


Exposure node name.




y


Outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




z


Character vector of instrument node names.




given


Character vector of node names the instruments are conditionally valid given (may be empty).

title: Validate instrumental variables
text:
Value
TRUE if z satisfies the instrumental variable criterion.

title: Validate instrumental variables
text:
Examples

# Classic IV graph: Z --> X --> Y with hidden confounder U --> X, U --> Y
dag <- cgraph(Z %-->% X, X %-->% Y, U %-->% X, U %-->% Y)
is_valid_iv(dag, "X", "Y", "Z") # Z is a valid instrument
#> [1] TRUE
is_valid_iv(dag, "X", "Y", "U") # U confounds X and Y
#> [1] FALSE

# W confounds Z and Y, so Z is an instrument only given W
dag <- cgraph(W %-->% Z + Y, Z %-->% X %-->% Y, U %-->% X + Y)
is_valid_iv(dag, "X", "Y", "Z")
#> [1] FALSE
is_valid_iv(dag, "X", "Y", "Z", given = "W")
#> [1] TRUE

title: Build the maximal local MAG for a local structure
text:
Description
Returns the maximal local MAG for the local structure c at x in the PAG cg.

title: Build the maximal local MAG for a local structure
text:
Usage
maximal_local_mag(cg, x, c)

title: Build the maximal local MAG for a local structure
text:
Arguments



cg


A PAG created with cgraph().




x


Node name.




c


Character vector of node names: a valid local structure at x.

title: Build the maximal local MAG for a local structure
text:
Details
This is cg with a bidirected edge from x to every node in c and a directed edge from x to every other circle-marked neighbor, treated as local background knowledge and closed under the corresponding rule set. c should be a valid local structure, i.e. an entry of what possible_local_structures() returns for x; passing an invalid one gives an unsound result. The returned graph may still contain circles, which is why it is returned as class "UNKNOWN" rather than validated as a MAG or PAG.
Assumes cg has no selection bias (no undirected edges).

text:

A cgraph of class UNKNOWN.

title: Build the maximal local MAG for a local structure
text:
References
Wang T, Qin T, Zhou Z (2023). “Sound and complete causal identification with latent variables given local background knowledge.” Artificial Intelligence, 322, 103964.
Wang T, Tao L, Qin T, Zhou Z (2025). “Estimating possible causal effects with latent variables via adjustment and novel rule orientation.” Artificial Intelligence, 347, 104387.

mag <- cgraph(
  A %<->% X, B %-->% X, A %<->% B, X %-->% Y,
  class = "MAG"

pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
maximal_local_mag(pag, "X", "A")
#> UNKNOWN with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, X, Y
#>   edges:
#>     A o-> B, A o-> X, X --> B, X --> Y

title: Generate a random graph
text: Source: R/construction.R

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Description
Generates a random graph on n observed nodes named V1, ..., Vn.

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Usage
generate_graph(
  n,
  m = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  class = c("DAG", "CPDAG", "ADMG", "MAG", "PAG"),
  latents = 0,
  seed = NULL
)

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Arguments



n


Number of observed nodes.




m


Number of edges (supply exactly one of m and p); drawn from the full n + latents node set when latents > 0.




p


Edge probability (supply exactly one of m and p); applied to the full n + latents node set when latents > 0.




class


Graph class: "DAG", "CPDAG", "ADMG", "MAG", or "PAG".




latents


Number of latent nodes to sample alongside the n observed nodes and then project out. Only supported for class = "ADMG", "MAG", or "PAG"; must be 0 (default) otherwise.




seed


Optional integer seed for reproducibility.

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Details
Edges are sampled uniformly at random over all possible pairs using Erdős–Rényi and oriented by a random topological ordering, guaranteeing acyclicity. This samples uniformly over graphs of a given size/density, but not uniformly over the space of DAGs (some DAGs correspond to more topological orderings than others). For an exact uniform draw from all labelled DAGs on n nodes regardless of edge count, use uniform_dag() instead.
Exactly one of m (exact edge count) or p (edge probability) must be given. For class = "CPDAG", the sampled DAG is converted with dag_to_cpdag(). For class = "ADMG", "MAG", or "PAG", latents additional nodes L1, ..., Lk are added to the underlying random DAG and then marginalized out via latent_project(); m/p are applied to the full n + latents node set before projection. latents must be 0 (the default) for class = "DAG" or class = "CPDAG".
Unlike ADMGs, MAGs (and PAGs, which are derived from a sampled MAG) additionally require the ancestral constraint (no bidirected edge between a node and its own ancestor), which a naive latent projection can violate whenever a marginalized common cause and a separate directed path connect the same pair of observed nodes. For class = "MAG" or class = "PAG", each candidate is checked and, if invalid, resampled (up to an internal retry limit) until a valid MAG is found; this errors if none is found, which can happen for very dense graphs with many latents. For class = "PAG", the resulting MAG is then converted to its equivalence class with mag_to_pag().

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Value
A cgraph.

title: Generate a random graph
text:
Examples

cg <- generate_graph(4, m = 3, seed = 1405)
cg
#> DAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: V1, V2, V3, V4
#>   edges:
#>     V2 --> V1, V2 --> V4, V3 --> V1

admg <- generate_graph(6, p = 0.3, class = "ADMG", latents = 2, seed = 1405)
admg
#> ADMG with 6 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: V1, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6
#>   edges:
#>     V1 --> V4, V2 --> V4

pag <- generate_graph(6, p = 0.3, class = "PAG", latents = 2, seed = 1405)
pag
#> PAG with 6 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: V1, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6
#>   edges:
#>     V1 o-> V4, V2 o-> V4

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text: Source: R/transform.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Description
Returns one MAG belonging to the Markov equivalence class represented by the PAG cg: a left inverse of mag_to_pag(), so mag_to_pag(mag_from_pag(pag)) recovers pag.

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Usage
mag_from_pag(cg)

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Arguments



cg


A PAG created with cgraph().

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Details
Every circle mark left unresolved by the PAG is resolved to a tail or arrowhead following Zhang’s construction (2008, Theorem 2): a circle opposite a fixed mark always becomes directed; an undirected edge (selection bias) is kept unchanged; the remaining all-circle edges form a chordal component, oriented into a DAG with no new unshielded colliders by Dor-Tarsi simplicial elimination.

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Value
A cgraph of class MAG.

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
References
Zhang J (2008). “On the completeness of orientation rules for causal discovery in the presence of latent confounders and selection bias.” Artificial Intelligence, 172(16-17), 1873–1896.
Dor D, Tarsi M (1992). “A simple algorithm to construct a consistent extension of a partially oriented graph.” Technical Report R-185, Cognitive Systems Laboratory, UCLA.

title: Resolve a PAG to a representative MAG
text:
Examples

pag <- cgraph(A %o-o% B, B %o-o% C, class = "PAG")
mag_from_pag(pag)
#> MAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     B --> A, C --> B

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text: Source: R/metrics.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Description
hd() is the skeleton Hamming distance: the number of node pairs on which cg1 and cg2 disagree about whether an edge is present, ignoring edge type and orientation. shd() is the Structural Hamming Distance: the number of node pairs on which they disagree at all, about the presence of an edge or about its marks, weighting both kinds of mismatch equally.

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Usage
hd(cg1, cg2, normalized = FALSE)

shd(cg1, cg2, normalized = FALSE)

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Arguments



cg1, cg2


Graphs created with cgraph(), of any class, with the same nodes.




normalized


If TRUE, divide by the number of node pairs, n * (n - 1) / 2, giving a value in [0, 1].

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Details
The two graphs must have the same nodes, but may be of different classes. SHD was originally defined for PDAGs; shd() extends it naturally to any pair of graphs.
To compare causal discovery algorithms against a known true graph, first convert the truth to the class the algorithms estimate: dag_to_cpdag() for algorithms returning a CPDAG (such as PC), mag_to_pag() for ones returning a PAG (such as FCI). Otherwise edges the algorithm correctly leaves unoriented count as mistakes. If an estimate is an MPDAG built from background knowledge, apply the same knowledge to the true CPDAG with apply_background_knowledge().

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Value
A number: the count of disagreeing node pairs, or its share of all node pairs if normalized = TRUE.

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
References
Tsamardinos I, Brown LE, Aliferis CF (2006). “The max-min hill-climbing Bayesian network structure learning algorithm.” Machine Learning, 65, 31–78. doi:10.1007/s10994-006-6889-7.

title: Hamming distances between two graphs
text:
Examples

chain <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C)
collider <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B)
hd(chain, collider) # same skeleton
#> [1] 0
shd(chain, collider) # B -- C is oriented differently
#> [1] 1
shd(chain, collider, normalized = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.3333333

It contains every vertex other than x for which there is a collider path between x and the vertex in cg on which every vertex, including the vertex itself, is an ancestor of x or of some member of y. backdoor_set() uses this set to build its generalized back-door set for a MAG or PAG.

title: Find an adjustment set
text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Description
Computes a valid adjustment set for the total causal effect of x on y.

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Usage
adjustment_set(
  cg,
  x,
  y,
  type = c("optimal", "parents", "backdoor"),
  include = character(),
  restrict = NULL
)

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG, ADMG, PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG), AG-family (AG, MAG), or PAG graph created with cgraph().




x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names (to identify the effect of a set of exposures on a set of outcomes).




type


Adjustment set type: "optimal" (default), "parents", or "backdoor". Ignored for ADMG, MAG-family, and PAG graphs; "backdoor" is not supported for PDAG-family graphs.




include


Character vector of nodes forced into the set.




restrict


Character vector of candidate nodes the set is drawn from. NULL (default) allows every node except x and y. include and restrict need type = "backdoor" for a DAG, and are not supported for PDAG-family graphs.

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Details
The supported adjustment set types depend on the graph class:


DAG


All three types are supported.


PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG)


Only "parents" and "optimal" are supported; "backdoor" raises an error.


ADMG, MAG-family (AG, MAG), PAG


type is ignored. The smallest valid adjustment set is returned by searching sets of increasing size.


The available adjustment set types are:


"parents"


The parents of x, excluding x and y.


"backdoor"


An inclusion-minimal set satisfying Pearl’s backdoor criterion: a minimal separator of x and y among x’s non-descendants, after removing x’s outgoing edges (falls back to the parents of x if no such separator is found).


"optimal"


The O-set: the parents of causal nodes on a possibly causal path from x to y, excluding x and those causal nodes themselves.


Candidate adjustment sets can be validated with is_valid_adjustment().

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Value
Character vector with a valid adjustment set, or NULL if none exists.

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
References
Henckel L, Perković E, Maathuis MH (2022). “Graphical Criteria for Efficient Total Effect Estimation Via Adjustment in Causal Linear Models.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 84, 579–599. ("optimal")
Pearl J (2009). Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference, 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press. ("parents" and "backdoor")

title: Find an adjustment set
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(
  C %-->% X, X %-->% F + D, A %-->% X + K, K %-->% Y,
  D %-->% Y + G, Y %-->% H
)
sort(adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "parents"))
#> [1] "A" "C"
adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "backdoor")
#> [1] "A"
adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "optimal") # default
#> [1] "K"

pdag <- cgraph(A %-->% X, X %-->% Y, A %-->% Y, class = "PDAG")
adjustment_set(pdag, "X", "Y") # A
#> [1] "A"
is_valid_adjustment(pdag, "X", "Y", "A")
#> [1] TRUE

mag <- cgraph(A %<->% X, A %-->% Y, X %-->% Y, class = "MAG")
adjustment_set(mag, "X", "Y") # A; type is ignored
#> NULL

# Only some nodes are observed
dag <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% X + Y, A %-->% Y, X %-->% Y)
adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "backdoor", restrict = c("A", "B"))
#> [1] "B"

text:
Description
For every pair of nodes non-adjacent in cg2, picks a set separating them in cg2, and counts the pairs that set fails to separate in cg1. This measures how far cg1 is from satisfying the independences cg2 implies, in the way a constraint-based analysis would test them.

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
Usage
separation_distance(
  cg1,
  cg2,
  strategy = c("parents", "ancestors", "zl"),
  mb_enhanced = FALSE,
  symmetric = FALSE,
  normalized = FALSE
)

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
Arguments



cg1


The graph the separating sets are tested in.




cg2


The graph the separating sets are read off: a DAG, PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG), AG-family (AG, MAG), or PAG graph created with cgraph(), of the same kind as cg1 and with the same nodes.




strategy


The separating set strategy for two DAGs: "parents" (default), "ancestors", or "zl". Not available for other classes.




mb_enhanced


If TRUE, use Markov blankets as separating sets where possible.




symmetric


If TRUE, average the distance over both directions.




normalized


If TRUE, divide by the number of node pairs, n * (n - 1) / 2, giving a value in [0, 1].

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
Details
The separating set is picked by class:


DAG


By strategy: "parents" (the parents of both nodes), "ancestors" (their ancestors), or "zl" (a minimal separator, as minimal_separator()).


AG, MAG, PAG


A minimal separator.


PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG


The possible parents of both nodes: their parents in any DAG consistent with cg2, which is invariant under Markov equivalence.


mb_enhanced = TRUE uses the Markov blanket of the first node instead wherever it separates them, which is often cheaper on sparse graphs.

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
Value
A number: the count of failed separations, or its share of all node pairs if normalized = TRUE.

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
References
Wahl J, Runge J (2025). “Separation-Based Distance Measures for Causal Graphs.” In Li Y, Mandt S, Agrawal S, Khan E (eds.), Proceedings of The 28th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, volume 258 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 3412–3420. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v258/wahl25b.html.

title: Separation distance between two graphs
text:
Examples

cg1 <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C, A %-->% C, C %-->% D)
cg2 <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C %-->% D)
separation_distance(cg1, cg2)
#> [1] 1
separation_distance(cg1, cg2, strategy = "zl")
#> [1] 2
separation_distance(cg1, cg2, symmetric = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.5

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text: Source: R/metrics.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Description
Compare two graphs by every separation statement (x, y, s) they imply, for every pair of nodes x, y and every set s of the other nodes with at most max_order nodes. The share of statements on which the graphs disagree is computed for each size of s, and the shares are averaged over the sizes, so that the many large sets do not dominate.

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Usage
sc_metric(cg1, cg2, max_order = NULL)

markov_metric(cg_truth, cg_test, max_order = NULL)

faithfulness_metric(cg_truth, cg_test, max_order = NULL)

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Arguments



cg1, cg2, cg_truth, cg_test


Graphs created with cgraph(), with the same nodes and the same notion of separation: both d-separation (DAG, PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) or both m-separation (ADMG, AG, MAG, PAG).




max_order


Maximum size of the separating sets. NULL (default) uses every size, up to n - 2.

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Details
sc_metric() counts every disagreement, so it is symmetric in its arguments. markov_metric() (the c-metric) counts only the statements connected in cg_truth but separated in cg_test, the false-negative rate for connections; it is 0 when cg_test is at least as connected as cg_truth. faithfulness_metric() (the s-metric) counts only the statements separated in cg_truth but connected in cg_test, the false-positive rate. A size with no statements of the counted kind contributes 0.
A graph and its equivalence class (e.g. dag_to_cpdag(), mag_to_pag()) imply the same separations, so, unlike shd() and aid(), these metrics need no conversion of the true graph when comparing causal discovery algorithms.
The number of statements grows exponentially with the number of nodes, so limit max_order for larger graphs.

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Value
A number in [0, 1].

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
References
Wahl J, Runge J (2025). “Separation-Based Distance Measures for Causal Graphs.” In Li Y, Mandt S, Agrawal S, Khan E (eds.), Proceedings of The 28th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, volume 258 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 3412–3420. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v258/wahl25b.html.

title: Separation/connection metrics between two graphs
text:
Examples

truth <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C %-->% D)
test <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B, C %-->% D)
sc_metric(truth, test)
#> [1] 0.25
sc_metric(truth, test, max_order = 0)
#> [1] 0.3333333
markov_metric(truth, test)
#> [1] 0.1527778
faithfulness_metric(truth, test)
#> [1] 0.2777778

x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




minimal

max_size


Maximum adjustment set size to consider.

title: Markov blanket of a node
text: Source: R/queries.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Description
Returns the Markov blanket of node in cg: the minimal set of nodes that renders node conditionally independent of every other node in the graph.

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Usage
markov_blanket(cg, node)

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG, PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG), ADMG, AG-family (AG, MAG), or PAG graph created with cgraph().




node


Node name.

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Details
Which nodes it contains depends on the graph class:


DAG: parents, children, and co-parents (other parents of node’s children).


PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG): the DAG set, plus undirected neighbors.


ADMG: the union of the parents of every node in node’s district (excluding node itself).


AG-family (AG, MAG): parents, children, co-parents, spouses, and undirected neighbors.


PAG: the AG-family set in the representative MAG of cg from mag_from_pag().

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Value
Sorted character vector of node names.

title: Markov blanket of a node
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %-->% C, D %-->% C)
markov_blanket(dag, "B") # A, C, D (D is a co-parent)
#> [1] "A" "C" "D"
markov_blanket(dag, "C")
#> [1] "B" "D"

title: Edge specification operators
text:
Description
Infix operators that specify edges inside cgraph(), add_edges(), remove_edges(), apply_background_knowledge(), and dag_to_mpdag(), e.g. A %-->% X + Y.

title: Edge specification operators
text:
Usage
lhs %-->% rhs

lhs %<--% rhs

lhs %---% rhs

lhs %<->% rhs

lhs %o->% rhs

lhs %<-o% rhs

lhs %o--% rhs

lhs %--o% rhs

lhs %o-o% rhs

lhs %!-->% rhs

lhs %!<--% rhs

title: Edge specification operators
text:
Arguments



lhs, rhs


Node name(s): a bare symbol, a string, or a +-combination or c() of either.

title: Edge specification operators
text:
Details
Use + for several nodes on one side: A %-->% X + Y means A --> X and A --> Y. Chaining connects consecutive nodes: X %-->% M %-->% Y means X --> M and M --> Y.



Operator


Meaning




%-->%


directed, src --> dst




%<--%


directed, dst --> src




%---%


undirected




%<->%


bidirected




%o->%


partially directed, src o-> dst




%<-o%


partially directed, dst o-> src




%o--%


partially undirected, src o-- dst




%--o%


partially undirected, dst o-- src




%o-o%


partial (both ends circle)



apply_background_knowledge() and dag_to_mpdag() also take %!-->% (src --> dst is forbidden) and %!<--% (dst --> src is forbidden), where %-->% and %<--% mean a required edge.
These functions read the operators from their ... without evaluating them. The operators are not exported, so they can’t be used anywhere else.

title: Edge specification operators
text:
Value
None, since the operators are never called.

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Description
Nodes adjacent to node by some edge. mode restricts which edge types count: "in" (parents / arrowheads at node), "out" (children / tails at node), "undirected", or "bidirected"; "all" (default) includes every neighbor regardless of edge type.

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Usage
neighbors(cg, node, mode = c("all", "in", "out", "undirected", "bidirected"))

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Arguments



cg


A graph created with cgraph(), of any class.




node


Node name.




mode


Which edge types to include: "all" (default), "in", "out", "undirected", or "bidirected".

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Details
For a PAG, "in", "out", "undirected", and "bidirected" only match definite (circle-free) edges; neighbors joined by a circle mark (o->, o--, o-o) are reported by "all" only.

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Value
Sorted character vector of node names.

title: Neighbors of a node
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B)
neighbors(dag, "B")
#> [1] "A" "C"
neighbors(dag, "B", mode = "in")
#> [1] "A" "C"
neighbors(dag, "A", mode = "out")
#> [1] "B"

text: Source: R/plot-compose.R

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Description
Style a plot built with cgraph_plot() one step at a time. Each function returns the plot, so the steps chain with |>, and the plot is drawn when it is printed. Passing a graph instead of a plot starts one with cgraph_plot()’s defaults.

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Usage
style_nodes(p, ..., nodes = NULL)

style_labels(p, ..., nodes = NULL)

style_title(p, ...)

label_nodes(p, ...)

style_edges(p, ..., from = NULL, to = NULL, type = NULL)

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Arguments



p


A plot from cgraph_plot(), or a graph created with cgraph().




...


Named style fields (see the sections below), or for label_nodes() the text to draw in each node, named by node, e.g. X = "Exposure"; \n starts a new line. Other nodes show their name.




nodes


Character vector of the nodes to style. NULL (default) styles every node.




from, to


Character vectors of nodes. An edge is styled if it joins a node in from to a node in to, in either direction unless type fixes it. NULL (default) allows any node.




type


Character vector of edge notations to style, read from a node in from to a node in to: "-->", "<--", "---", "<->", "o->", "<-o", "o--", "--o", or "o-o". NULL (default) allows every type. For example, from = "X", type = "-->" styles the edges out of X, and type = "<->" every bidirected edge.

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Details
Each call styles only the nodes or edges it selects. A later call wins over an earlier one for the fields both set, and anything left unset uses the defaults of plot_options(). The selectors take node sets, so the results of query functions such as parents() or adjustment_set() can be passed straight in.

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Value
The plot, a cgraph_plot object.

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Node fields (style_nodes())


fill, col: fill and border color.


lwd, linestyle: border width and line type (any lty).


shape: "circle", "square", "ellipse", or "rect".


radius: node size in mm. Unset, nodes fit their labels, with padding mm around the text, times size.

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Edge fields (style_edges())


col, lwd, lty: line color, width and type.


fill: arrowhead fill, by default the edge’s col; NA for hollow.


arrow_size, circle_size: arrowhead length and endpoint circle radius, in mm.


gap: space in mm between the edge ends and the nodes.


curvature: how far the edge bows; positive to the left travelling from its first node to its second, as listed by edges(). 0 turns off the automatic routing around nodes in the way.


path: waypoints the edge passes through, in layout coordinates, from the node in from to the node in to: a c(x, y) point, a two-column matrix, a data.frame with x and y columns, or a list of points.


label: text drawn along the edge, styled with label_col, label_fontsize, label_fontface and label_fontfamily, and placed with label_shift (0 at the edge’s first node to 1 at its second), label_distance (mm from the edge) and label_rotation (degrees; unset, it follows the edge).

title: Style the nodes, edges and labels of a plot
text:
Text fields (style_labels(), style_title())
col, fontsize, fontface, fontfamily, and cex.

cgraph_plot() for the layout and title, plot_options() for the defaults.
Other plotting: cgraph_grob(), cgraph_layout(), cgraph_plot(), cgraph_plot_grid(), plot_default_options(), plot_options()

text: Source: R/identification.R

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Description
id() returns the interventional distribution P(y | do(x)) as a formula in terms of the observational distribution, or NULL if the effect is not identifiable. It implements Shpitser & Pearl’s ID algorithm. idc() additionally conditions on given (the IDC algorithm), reducing to id() when given is empty.

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Usage
id(cg, x, y)

idc(cg, x, y, given = character())

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph().




x, y


Intervention (exposure) and outcome node name, or character vector of node names. Must be disjoint from each other (and from given, for idc()).




given


Character vector of node names to additionally condition on (idc() only).

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Details
Bidirected edges represent latent confounders. To identify an effect in a DAG with unobserved variables, project them out first with latent_project().
The rendered formula may mention variables outside x/y/given: the algorithm can enlarge the intervention set whenever doing so provably changes nothing, and the result is then a function of those extra values too.

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Value
A character scalar with the rendered formula, or NULL if the effect is not identifiable.

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
References
Shpitser I, Pearl J (2008). “Complete Identification Methods for the Causal Hierarchy.” Journal of Machine Learning Research, 9, 1941–1979.
Tian J, Pearl J (2002). “A General Identification Condition for Causal Effects.” In Proceedings of the 18th National Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2002), 567–573.

title: Identify an interventional distribution
text:
Examples

# Back-door adjustment, recovered as the g-formula
dag <- cgraph(Z %-->% X, X %-->% Y, Z %-->% Y)
id(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{Z} P(Y | X, Z) P(Z)"

# Front-door graph: X and Y are confounded, but the effect is still
# identifiable through the mediator M
admg <- cgraph(X %-->% M, M %-->% Y, X %<->% Y, class = "ADMG")
id(admg, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{M} P(M | X) (Σ_{X'} P(X') P(Y | M, X'))"

# The bow arc: the canonical unidentifiable effect
bow <- cgraph(X %-->% Y, X %<->% Y, class = "ADMG")
is.null(id(bow, "X", "Y"))
#> [1] TRUE

dag <- cgraph(Z %-->% X, X %-->% Y, Z %-->% Y)
idc(dag, "X", "Y", given = "Z")
#> [1] "P(Y | X, Z)"

title: Getting Started
text:
Source: vignettes/CausalStructures.qmd
This guide shows the basic usage of CausalStructures with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs).
library(CausalStructures)

title: Getting Started
text:
Constructing a graph
Let’s build a DAG with a confounder A that affects both X and Y, and a mediator M between X and Y:

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y, class = "DAG")
dag
#> DAG with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, M, X, Y
#>   edges:
#>     A --> X, A --> Y, X --> M, M --> Y

Each edge is written with an operator such as %-->%, %<->% or %o-o% (see edge operators), and + fans an edge out to, or in from, several nodes at once. class says which kind of graph it is; "DAG" is the default (see Graph Classes for the others).






NoteValidation on construction



Every graph is checked against the structural constraints of its class when you construct it. For a DAG, this means all edges are directed (%-->%) and there are no cycles. Let’s try to create a DAG with a cycle:

invalid_dag <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C %-->% A)
#> Error:
#> ! Invalid DAG:
#>   - directed cycles are not allowed in DAG



Since a picture is worth a thousand words1, let’s plot our DAG:

plot(dag)








For more plotting details and customization options, see Plotting Causal Graphs.

title: Getting Started
text:
Testing conditional independence
A central question in causal inference is whether two variables are conditionally independent. For DAGs, this is determined using d-separation.
Are X and Y independent?

d_separated(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] FALSE

No, there is a directed path X --> M --> Y.
If we condition on the mediator M, does that make them independent?

d_separated(dag, "X", "Y", given = "M")
#> [1] FALSE

Still no, the backdoor path via A, X <-- A --> Y, remains open.
What if we condition on both A and M?

d_separated(dag, "X", "Y", given = c("A", "M"))
#> [1] TRUE

Yes, now all paths are blocked.

title: Getting Started
text:
Finding adjustment sets
Now suppose we want to estimate the causal effect of X on Y. The backdoor path X <-- A --> Y introduces confounding bias, so we need to block it by conditioning on a valid adjustment set.
Let’s find one automatically:

adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "A"

We can also verify that a specific set is valid:

is_valid_adjustment(dag, "X", "Y", "A")
#> [1] TRUE

And enumerate all minimal valid adjustment sets:

all_adjustment_sets(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "A"

In this case, {A} is the only minimal set that blocks the confounding.

title: Getting Started
text:
Next steps
This quick guide barely scratched the surface of what you can do with this package:

For more on working with DAGs in the context of causal identification, see Causal Identification.
For what each graph class means and how to build one, see Graph Classes; for working with equivalence classes, see Equivalence Classes and PAG Causal Effects.
To customize plots, see Plotting Causal Graphs.

title: Getting Started
text:
Footnotes


Especially with causal graphs.↩︎

title: Causal Identification
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/causal-identification.qmd
This guide expands on the Getting Started guide with more advanced identification techniques.
library(CausalStructures)

title: Causal Identification
text:
Adjustment strategies
adjustment_set() supports three different strategies for finding adjustment sets. Let’s build a DAG with multiple confounders and mediators, Figure 6.5 of Peters et al. (2017):

dag <- cgraph(
  C %-->% X,
  A %-->% X + K,
  X %-->% F + D,
  K %-->% Y,
  D %-->% Y + G,
  Y %-->% H
)
plot(dag)








Parents strategy: Adjusts for all parents of X. Simple but often includes unnecessary variables:

adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "parents")
#> [1] "A" "C"

Backdoor strategy: Applies Pearl’s backdoor criterion to find valid adjustment sets that block all confounding paths:

adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "backdoor")
#> [1] "A"

Optimal strategy (default): Computes the O-set, which minimizes the asymptotic variance of the causal effect estimator:

adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y", type = "optimal")
#> [1] "K"

title: Causal Identification
text:
Minimal separator
Sometimes we need the smallest set of variables that d-separates two nodes. minimal_separator() finds one:

minimal_separator(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "A" "D"

The restrict argument limits the search to a specific pool of variables:

minimal_separator(dag, "X", "Y", restrict = c("D", "K"))
#> [1] "D" "K"

The include argument forces certain variables to always be in the result:

minimal_separator(dag, "X", "Y", include = "K")
#> [1] "D" "K"

title: Causal Identification
text:
Frontdoor adjustment
When confounders are unobserved, the backdoor criterion doesn’t apply. Consider a graph where an unobserved confounder U affects both the treatment X and outcome Y:

dag2 <- cgraph(U %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y)
plot(dag2)








The mediator M is a descendant of X, so adjusting for it violates the backdoor criterion:

is_valid_backdoor(dag2, "X", "Y", "M")
#> [1] FALSE

However, M intercepts every causal path from X to Y and is itself unconfounded; this is exactly the frontdoor criterion:

is_valid_frontdoor(dag2, "X", "Y", "M")
#> [1] TRUE


frontdoor_set(dag2, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "M"

title: Causal Identification
text:
Instrumental variables
When hidden confounders block backdoor adjustment and no suitable mediator exists for the frontdoor criterion, an instrumental variable (IV) can still identify the causal effect. An instrument Z must satisfy two conditions: it must be associated with the treatment X (relevance), and it can only affect the outcome Y through X (exclusion restriction).
Consider a graph where U is an unobserved confounder and Z is an available instrument, but there is no mediator on the path from X to Y:

dag3 <- cgraph(U %-->% X + Y, Z %-->% X %-->% Y)
plot(dag3)








Without a mediator, the frontdoor criterion cannot apply here:

is_valid_frontdoor(dag3, "X", "Y", "Z")
#> [1] FALSE

However, Z is a valid instrument since it is d-connected to X, and d-separated from Y once the causal edge X --> Y is removed, so it can only affect Y through X:

is_valid_iv(dag3, "X", "Y", "Z")
#> [1] TRUE

An instrument may also only be valid conditionally on a set of variables. Here W confounds Z and Y, so Z is an instrument only once we condition on W:

dag5 <- cgraph(W %-->% Z + Y, Z %-->% X %-->% Y, U %-->% X + Y)
is_valid_iv(dag5, "X", "Y", "Z")
#> [1] FALSE
is_valid_iv(dag5, "X", "Y", "Z", given = "W")
#> [1] TRUE

iv_set() searches for an instrument together with a conditioning set that makes it valid, and restrict limits both to the observed variables:

iv_set(dag5, "X", "Y")
#> $z
#> [1] "Z"
#> 
#> $given
#> [1] "W"
is.null(iv_set(dag5, "X", "Y", restrict = c("Z", "X", "Y")))
#> [1] TRUE

title: Causal Identification
text:
ADMG adjustment
In an ADMG (acyclic directed mixed graph), bidirected edges <-> represent hidden common causes directly, without explicitly keeping the unobserved nodes in the graph. An ADMG arises naturally by projecting unobserved variables out of a DAG with latent_project(). Let’s project U out of dag3:

admg <- latent_project(dag3, "U")
admg
#> ADMG with 3 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     X --> Y, X <-> Y, Z --> X

Removing U introduces X <-> Y, which captures its confounding effect. The functions discussed above also work on ADMGs, e.g.:

is_valid_iv(admg, "X", "Y", "Z")
#> [1] TRUE

title: Causal Identification
text:
General identification
The methods discussed above are each sufficient, not necessary. CausalStructures also implements the ID algorithm of Shpitser and Pearl (2008), which returns the estimand as a formula.
On a graph with an observed confounder, it recovers the familiar g-formula:

dag4 <- cgraph(Z %-->% X + Y, X %-->% Y)
id(dag4, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{Z} P(Y | X, Z) P(Z)"

Unlike the criteria above, id() also works when no adjustment set exists at all. Recall the front-door graph from before, where U is an unobserved confounder of X and Y, and M mediates the effect of X on Y. Projecting U out gives an ADMG with no valid adjustment set, yet id() still identifies the effect through the mediator:

admg2 <- latent_project(dag2, "U")
id(admg2, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{M} P(M | X) (Σ_{X'} P(X') P(Y | M, X'))"

which is the standard front-door adjustment formula. The primed X' is a summation index distinct from the intervened value of X, following the usual convention.
id() can also detect non-identifiability. In the instrument graph from before, with U projected out, the causal effect cannot be identified:

is.null(id(admg, "X", "Y"))
#> [1] TRUE

idc() extends id() to conditional effects \(P(y \mid do(x), z)\):

idc(admg2, "X", "Y", given = "M")
#> [1] "Σ_{X'} P(X') P(Y | M, X')"

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/plot.qmd
cgraph_plot() draws a cgraph with grid graphics. For node placement, you can use the layouts provided by Sugiyama.jl or NetworkLayout.jl1, or provide your own layout.
library(CausalStructures)

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Basic usage
You can pass any cgraph to cgraph_plot(), and all edge marks are supported:

unknown <- cgraph("A <-> B o-> C o-- A", class = "UNKNOWN")
cgraph_plot(unknown)








As an example, here is the DAG from Figure 6.5 of Peters, Janzing and Schölkopf (2017):

dag <- cgraph(
  "C --> X, A --> X + K, X --> F + D, K --> Y, D --> Y + G, Y --> H"
)
cgraph_plot(dag)








cgraph_plot() returns a cgraph_plot object, which is drawn when it is printed. At the console that happens automatically; inside a function or loop, call print() on it. plot(dag) is a shortcut that builds the plot and draws it right away.

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Styling a plot
Before a plot is drawn, you can add styling to it step by step, chained with |>:

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(col = "gray60") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightskyblue", nodes = "Y") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", lwd = 2, from = "K", to = "Y")








There are five style functions:

style_nodes() styles the nodes in nodes.
style_edges() styles the edges joining a node in from to a node in to, optionally of a given type.
style_labels() styles the node labels in nodes, and label_nodes() sets their text.
style_title() styles the title.

Each call styles only the nodes or edges it selects; leaving out a selector selects everything. If two calls set the same field, the later one wins, so you can start with a style for all edges, as above, and then single some out.
Since the selectors are node sets, you can pass the results of query functions straight in. For example, to highlight the parents of Y and dash the edges into it:

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightskyblue", nodes = parents(dag, "Y")) |>
  style_edges(lty = "dashed", to = "Y", type = "-->")








A style function also accepts a graph directly, starting the plot with the default layout, so dag |> style_nodes(fill = "gold") works too.
If you want to set defaults for an entire project, you can use plot_options(), with a list of fields for each of node_style, edge_style, label_style and title_style. The style functions still take precedence, and plot_options(plot_default_options()) resets to the built-in defaults:
plot_options(node_style = list(fill = "lightblue"), edge_style = list(lwd = 2))
cgraph_grob() gives the grid grob of a plot, if you want to draw it yourself with grid::grid.draw(), for example in a viewport of a larger figure.

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Layout
The layout argument controls where the nodes are placed. It defaults to "sugiyama" for a DAG, and to "stress" otherwise.

cgraph_plot(dag, layout = "stress")








You can use these names for the built-in layouts. "sugiyama" comes from Sugiyama.jl, while the others come from NetworkLayout.jl, as in CausalStructures.jl; see ?cgraph_layout for details:



layout
Algorithm




"sugiyama"
Sugiyama (layered) layout


"stress"
Stress majorization


"spring"
Fruchterman-Reingold force-directed


"sfdp"
Scalable force-directed placement


"spectral"
Spectral layout


"shell"
Nodes evenly spaced on a circle


"squaregrid"
Square grid



"stress", "spring" and "sfdp" start from random positions; seed (default 1) makes them reproducible.
For "sugiyama", direction ("right", the default, "down", "up", or "left") sets which way the layers flow:

cgraph_plot(dag, direction = "down")








If you want to place the nodes yourself, you can pass explicit positions instead of a name. You can either use a named list of c(x, y) pairs keyed by node name, or a data.frame with name, x, and y columns:

cgraph_plot(
  dag,
  layout = list(
    A = c(0, 1),
    C = c(0, -1),
    K = c(1, 1),
    X = c(1, -1),
    D = c(2, -1),
    F = c(2, -2),
    Y = c(3, 0),
    G = c(3, 1),
    H = c(4, 0)
  )
)














TipTweaking a layout by hand



You can compute a starting layout using cgraph_layout(), and then manually adjust a few nodes:

positions <- cgraph_layout(dag, method = "stress")
positions[positions$name == "G", c("x", "y")] <- c(1, 1.5)
cgraph_plot(dag, layout = positions)
















TipSugiyama positions without Sugiyama routing



Sugiyama.jl implements its own routing using dummy nodes. If you prefer the automatic Bezier-curve routing used otherwise, you can compute the Sugiyama positions with cgraph_layout() and pass those instead:

dag_layered <- cgraph("A --> X, A --> B, X --> Y, B --> Y, A --> Y")
cgraph_plot(dag_layered, layout = cgraph_layout(dag_layered, "sugiyama"))

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Styling nodes
style_nodes() takes these fields:








Field
Default
Controls




fill
"white"
fill color


col
"black"
border color


lwd
1
border line width


linestyle
solid
border line style (any lty)


shape
"circle"
node outline shape


radius
NULL (text-fit)
size of each node (mm)


padding
2
clearance (mm) around each label when radius is NULL


size
1
multiplier on the computed node size



Combine color, border, and shape to highlight a node:

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightblue", col = "navy") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "salmon", col = "#DC143C", nodes = "A") |>
  style_nodes(shape = "square", nodes = "K")








You can set shape to "circle" (the default), "square", "ellipse", or "rect". The latter two are mainly useful when you want to fit an oblong label. You can also use linestyle to style the border, for example to mark a latent variable:

dag |> style_nodes(linestyle = "dashed", col = "gray50", nodes = "X")








If you only want to draw the node names, you can make the fill and the border transparent. Edges still stop at the (now invisible) node boundary, so you can use "rect" with a smaller padding to bring the arrowheads closer to the text:

dag |>
  style_nodes(
    fill = "transparent",
    col = "transparent",
    shape = "rect",
    padding = 1
  )









Text-fit node sizing
By default (radius = NULL), nodes are sized to fit their labels:

longlabels <- cgraph("Exposure --> Mediator --> Y_outcome")
longlabels |> style_nodes(shape = "ellipse", nodes = "Exposure")








If you want to control the size yourself, you can set radius explicitly:

dag |> style_nodes(radius = 6)

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Styling edges
style_edges() selects the edges joining a node in from to a node in to, in either direction. type keeps only the edges with the given notation, read from from to to, so it also fixes the direction:







Call
Styles




style_edges(p, ...)
every edge


style_edges(p, ..., from = "X")
every edge touching X


style_edges(p, ..., from = "X", type = "-->")
the edges out of X


style_edges(p, ..., to = "X", type = "-->")
the edges into X


style_edges(p, ..., from = "A", to = "X")
the edges between A and X


style_edges(p, ..., type = "<->")
every bidirected edge



The notations are "-->", "<--", "---", "<->", "o->", "<-o", "o--", "--o", and "o-o". style_edges() takes these fields:








Field
Default
Controls




col
"black"
line / marker color


fill
NULL (the edge’s col)
arrowhead fill color


lwd
1
line width


lty
solid
line style


gap
0
gap (mm) at edge ends


curvature
NULL
how far the edge bows


path
NULL
explicit waypoints for an edge’s route


arrow_size
3
length (mm) of arrowhead triangles


circle_size
1.5
radius (mm) of open-circle (o) endpoints



Let’s style some edges by type:

admg <- cgraph("X --> Y, X <-> Z, Z --> Y", class = "ADMG")

cgraph_plot(admg) |>
  style_edges(col = "steelblue", type = "-->") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", lwd = 2.5, type = "<->")








fill controls the arrowhead’s fill color. By default (NULL), it uses the edge’s resolved col, so arrowheads are solid. If you want hollow, outline-only arrowheads, pass NA:

dag |> style_edges(fill = NA)








lty styles the edge line itself. For example, you can use it to dash <-> edges:

admg |> style_edges(lty = "dashed", type = "<->")








If you prefer some space between each end of an edge and the node border, you can set gap:

dag |> style_edges(gap = 1)









Parallel edges
If an ADMG has both X --> Y and X <-> Y, from = "X", to = "Y" selects both edges. If you need to distinguish them, add type:

shared <- cgraph("X --> Y, X <-> Y", class = "ADMG")

cgraph_plot(shared) |>
  style_edges(col = "steelblue") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", from = "X", to = "Y", type = "<->")








Notice that the two edges between X and Y are automatically curved apart, so they don’t overlap.


Curvature and automatic routing
curvature bows an edge into an arc instead of drawing it straight. Positive values bow the edge to the left when travelling from its first node to its second (as listed by edges()), while negative values bow it to the right.

admg |> style_edges(curvature = -0.3, type = "<->")








If a straight edge would pass too close to a non-incident node, it is automatically bent around that node with a Bezier curve. Edges with nothing in the way are always drawn straight.

detour <- cgraph("A --> X + Y, X --> Y")

cgraph_plot(detour, layout = list(A = c(0, 0), X = c(1, 0), Y = c(2, 0)))








If you want to disable this automatic routing for a particular edge, you can set its curvature to 0:

cgraph_plot(detour, layout = list(A = c(0, 0), X = c(1, 0), Y = c(2, 0))) |>
  style_edges(curvature = 0, from = "A", to = "Y")










Explicit edge paths
Edges are normally drawn as straight lines unless automatic routing is needed. If you want to control the path yourself, you can set path and provide intermediate points for the edge, in the coordinates of the layout. For example, the edge K --> Y below is drawn through the point (0.5, -0.25):

positions <- cgraph_layout(dag, method = "stress")

cgraph_plot(dag, layout = positions) |>
  style_edges(path = c(0.5, -0.25), from = "K", to = "Y")








For several points, path can also be a two-column matrix, a data.frame with x and y columns, or a list of c(x, y) points, listed from the node in from to the node in to.

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Labels and titles

Labels
By default, each node is labelled with its own name. If you want different labels, you can set them with label_nodes(). Node sizing takes multi-line labels into account, so the nodes grow to fit:

cgraph("A0 --> L1 --> A1 --> Y, A0 --> Y + A1") |>
  label_nodes(
    A0 = "Treatment\nat baseline",
    L1 = "Confounder\nat time 1",
    A1 = "Treatment\nat time 1"
  )








style_labels() styles the label text of the nodes in nodes:



Field
Default
Controls




col
"black"
text color


fontsize
10
font size


fontface
"plain"
font face


fontfamily
""
font family




cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_labels(fontsize = 13) |>
  style_labels(col = "#DC143C", nodes = "A")










Edge labels
Edge labels are set with style_edges(), so they select edges in the same way as edge styling.








Field
Default
Controls




label
NULL
text drawn along the edge


label_col
"black"
edge label text color


label_fontsize
9
edge label font size


label_fontface
"plain"
edge label font face


label_fontfamily
""
edge label font family


label_shift
0.5
position along the edge, 0 (first node) to 1 (second node)


label_distance
NULL
perpendicular gap (mm) from the edge; NULL scales with label_fontsize


label_rotation
NULL
text angle in degrees; NULL follows the edge’s own angle



Let’s add a label to the edge K --> Y:

dag |> style_edges(label = "hello", from = "K", to = "Y")








By default, the label follows the edge’s angle. You can use label_shift and label_distance to move it along or away from the edge:

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(label_shift = 0.75, label_distance = 4) |>
  style_edges(label = "hi", from = "K", to = "Y")








If an edge is steep or curved, following its angle can make the label hard to read. You can use label_rotation to give it a fixed angle instead:

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(
    label = "steep",
    label_rotation = 0,
    label_distance = 6,
    label_col = "#DC143C",
    from = "A",
    to = "X"
  ) |>
  style_edges(label = "follows", from = "K", to = "Y")










Titles
If you want to add a title, set main, and style it with style_title(), which takes the same fields as style_labels():








Argument / field
Default
Controls




main
NULL
plot title; NULL means no title


fontsize
14
title font size


col
"black"
title color


fontface
"bold"
title font face


title_gap
grid::unit(1, "lines")
gap between the title and the graph




cgraph_plot(dag, main = "My DAG") |>
  style_title(fontsize = 20, col = "navy")

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Figure size and margins








Argument
Default
Controls




outer_margin
grid::unit(2, "mm")
padding around the whole plot


asp
NA
y/x aspect ratio of the layout; NA fills the available space



A plot is drawn into whatever graphics device is open, so the figure size is set the usual R way, e.g. with grDevices::png(width =, height =) or a chunk’s fig-width/fig-height. Let’s make the figure a bit larger:

cgraph_plot(dag)







Figure 1











TipLarge graphs need a bigger figure



The default figure size works well for small examples. As your graph gets larger, labels and edges can become cramped or overlap. Increase the figure size (and, if needed, the node radius or the label fontsize) to keep larger graphs readable.








TipUneven figure sizes and asp



By default, node positions are stretched to fill the figure, which can distort the layout’s own proportions in an uneven figure. If you want to keep them instead, set asp = 1.

title: Plotting Causal Graphs
text:
Several plots in one figure
Plots combine with | (side by side) and / (stacked). Let’s draw the DAG and the ADMG side by side:

cgraph_plot(dag, main = "DAG") |
  style_nodes(cgraph_plot(admg, main = "ADMG"), fill = "salmon")








A chain of one operator gives equal panels (p1 | p2 | p3), and the two nest: (p1 | p2) / p3 puts two plots above a third. Style each plot before combining it, since the style verbs act on a single graph.
For more plots, or a list of them, cgraph_plot_grid() arranges them in rows and columns, with optional relative widths and heights:

dags <- lapply(1:6, function(i) generate_graph(5, p = 0.4, seed = i))
cgraph_plot_grid(lapply(dags, cgraph_plot), ncol = 3)








The gap between plots is plot_options("spacing"), or the spacing argument of cgraph_plot_grid().

Into an existing figure
A plot (or an arrangement) printed with newpage = FALSE is drawn into the current grid viewport instead of a new page, e.g. as one panel of a larger grid figure. cgraph_grob() gives its grid grob, which also lets you combine it with ggplot2 plots through patchwork:

patchwork::wrap_elements(full = cgraph_grob(cgraph_plot(dag))) + my_ggplot
