title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/pag-causal-effects.qmd
This guide builds on Equivalence Classes and Causal Identification and covers causal adjustment when the graph is known only as a PAG, i.e. when the underlying MAG is identified only up to Markov equivalence.
library(CausalStructures)

title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
Adjustment with a PAG
Consider the MAG from Equivalence Classes, where A and B share a hidden common cause, and C and B each cause their successor, with an added direct effect A --> D:

mag <- cgraph(A %<->% B, C %-->% B %-->% D, A %-->% D, class = "MAG")
pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
plot(pag)








The resulting PAG contains the circle-marked edge A o-> B. Depending on which MAG in the equivalence class is the true graph, this edge can correspond to either A --> B or A <-> B.
Consequently, backdoor_set() cannot determine an adjustment set from the PAG alone:

is.null(backdoor_set(pag, "A", "D"))
#> [1] TRUE

In particular, whether B needs to be included in an adjustment set depends on how the circle at A is resolved.
Not every effect here is uncertain. For the effect of B on D, the PAG admits an adjustment set that is valid for every MAG in the equivalence class. The generalized adjustment criterion (GAC) can therefore be applied directly to the PAG with all_adjustment_sets():

all_adjustment_sets(pag, "B", "D", minimal = FALSE)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "A"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "A" "C"

title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
Adjustment sets
pagcauses() considers MAGs compatible with the PAG and returns adjustment sets that are valid in at least one such MAG (Wang et al. 2025):

pagcauses(pag, "A", "D")
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "B"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "B" "C"

For this example, the empty set is valid when A --> B, since there is then no backdoor path from A to D through B. When A <-> B, B must instead be included to block the path through the hidden common cause. Thus {B} is a valid adjustment set in that case; nonminimal supersets such as {B, C} may also be returned when they are valid.
The same procedure applies when the ambiguity occurs elsewhere in the graph. For example:

pagcauses(pag, "C", "D")
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)

If there is no MAG compatible with the PAG in which D can have a causal effect on A, pagcauses() returns no possible causal effect:

pagcauses(pag, "D", "A")
#> list()

This is consistent with possible_ancestors().






NoteNo selection bias



pagcauses(), possible_local_structures(), and maximal_local_mag() assume that the PAG has no selection bias, matching the assumptions in the source papers. Selection bias shows up as an undirected edge in a PAG, and all three functions throw an error if the PAG has one:

selection_pag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C %---% D %---% A, class = "PAG")
pagcauses(selection_pag, "A", "B")
#> Error:
#> ! pagcauses (Wang, Tao, Qin & Zhou 2025) assumes no selection variables (no undirected edges)









NoteWhy not just enumerate the MAGs?



One could enumerate all MAGs with enumerate_mags() and apply backdoor_set() to each one. However, the number of MAGs in a Markov equivalence class grows as \(O(3^{(d^2-d)/2})\) with the number of nodes \(d\).
pagcauses() avoids constructing these MAGs. Instead, it uses graphical conditions to check whether a candidate adjustment set can be valid for a MAG compatible with the PAG. This reduces the complexity to \(O(5^d d^6)\) (Wang et al. 2025, sec. 3.4).
Depending on your graph size, the brute force approach could of course still be faster in practice.

title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
Local structures
pagcauses() builds on a smaller graphical primitive: possible_local_structures(). For a single node x, this function enumerates which subsets of its circle-marked neighbors could resolve to x <-> v, with the remaining circle-marked edges resolving to x --> v, in some consistent MAG (Wang et al. 2023):

possible_local_structures(pag, "A")
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "B"

A has one circle-marked neighbor, B, so there are two local structures: the empty set, corresponding to A --> B, and {B}, corresponding to A <-> B. Pairing a local structure with maximal_local_mag() resolves the edges around A implied by this local background knowledge:

maximal_local_mag(pag, "A", character())
#> UNKNOWN with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, A --> D, C o-> B, B --> D


maximal_local_mag(pag, "A", "B")
#> UNKNOWN with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A <-> B, A --> D, C o-> B, B --> D

These correspond to the two cases considered by pagcauses(pag, "A", "D"): the first gives {} as a valid adjustment set for A and D, while the second gives {B}. The result is returned as an UNKNOWN graph rather than a MAG, since local background knowledge about one node need not resolve every circle in the graph.

title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
General identification
The methods above are each sufficient, not necessary: an effect can be identifiable even when no adjustment set exists. idp() and cidp() implement the IDP/CIDP algorithms of Jaber et al. (2022), the PAG analogues of id() and idc() (see General identification): they decide identifiability of \(P(y \mid do(x))\) and \(P(y \mid do(x), z)\) from a PAG and, when identifiable, return the estimand.
Consider a MAG where A confounds X, B --> X, and X causes Y, and view its Markov equivalence class:

mag3 <- cgraph(B %-->% X, A %<->% X, A %-->% Y, X %-->% Y, class = "MAG")
pag3 <- mag_to_pag(mag3)
plot(pag3)








We can then check whether the effect of X on Y is identifiable with idp():

idp(pag3, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "Σ_{A, B} (P(A, B, X, Y) / P(X | A, B))"

The effect is identifiable, and conditioning on A also identifies the conditional effect:

cidp(pag3, "X", "Y", given = "A")
#> [1] "(Σ_{B} (P(A, B, X, Y) / P(X | A, B))) / P(A)"

title: PAG Causal Effects
text:
References


Jaber, Amin, Adele Ribeiro, Jiji Zhang, and Elias Bareinboim. 2022. “Causal Identification Under Markov Equivalence: Calculus, Algorithm, and Completeness.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, edited by S. Koyejo, S. Mohamed, A. Agarwal, D. Belgrave, K. Cho, and A. Oh, vol. 35. Curran Associates, Inc. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-0266.


Wang, Tian-Zuo, Tian Qin, and Zhi-Hua Zhou. 2023. “Sound and Complete Causal Identification with Latent Variables Given Local Background Knowledge.” Artificial Intelligence 322: 103964.


Wang, Tian-Zuo, Lue Tao, Tian Qin, and Zhi-Hua Zhou. 2025. “Estimating Possible Causal Effects with Latent Variables via Adjustment and Novel Rule Orientation.” Artificial Intelligence 347: 104387.

title: Graph Classes
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/graph-classes.qmd
This guide explains how to build a causal graph and what each graph class means. For a full introduction to these graphs and the theory behind them, see, for instance, Pearl (2009) or Peters et al. (2017); Richardson and Spirtes (2002) cover ancestral graphs (AGs and MAGs) specifically, and Zhang (2008) covers PAGs.
library(CausalStructures)

title: Graph Classes
text:
Constructing graphs
cgraph() builds a graph from edges written with infix operators, and its class argument ("DAG" by default) sets the graph class:

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y)
admg <- cgraph(X %-->% Y, X %<->% Y, class = "ADMG")

Each operator is an edge with a mark at either end: a tail (-), an arrowhead (< or >) or a circle (o).



Operator
Edge




%-->%
directed, src --> dst


%<--%
directed, dst --> src


%---%
undirected


%<->%
bidirected


%o->%
partially directed, src o-> dst


%<-o%
partially directed, dst o-> src


%o--%
partially undirected, src o-- dst


%--o%
partially undirected, dst o-- src


%o-o%
partial (circles at both ends)



+ fans an edge out to (or in from) several nodes at once, and chaining operators connects consecutive groups of nodes, so A %-->% B %-->% C gives the two edges A --> B and B --> C, while A %-->% B + C gives A --> B and A --> C. A bare node name declares an isolated node:

nodes(cgraph(A %-->% B, F))
#> [1] "A" "B" "F"

To build a graph from a string made at run time, pass the same edges as a string through spec, with the operators written without %:

spec <- paste("A -->", paste0("X", 1:3, collapse = " + "))
edges(cgraph(spec = spec))
#>   from to type
#> 1    A X1  -->
#> 2    A X2  -->
#> 3    A X3  -->

title: Graph Classes
text:
Graph classes
Each class is checked on construction, so a graph of a class is always valid for it. Building a DAG with a cycle, or with a bidirected edge, is an error:

cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C %-->% A)
#> Error:
#> ! Invalid DAG:
#>   - directed cycles are not allowed in DAG
cgraph(A %<->% B)
#> Error:
#> ! Invalid DAG:
#>   - invalid edge type for graph class DAG

reclass() changes the class of an existing graph, again checking the result, and the predicates (is_dag(), is_cpdag(), is_mag(), …) test whether a graph satisfies a class’s constraints, independent of its own graph class.

Directed acyclic graphs
A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is the standard causal graph. All edges are directed (-->), and the graph contains no directed cycles. An edge X --> Y means X is a direct cause of Y.


Partially directed acyclic graphs
The PDAG family ("PDAG", "CPDAG", "MPDAG") has directed (-->) and undirected (---) edges, and no directed cycles. An undirected edge is one whose orientation is not specified.

A PDAG is the general case.
A CPDAG represents a whole Markov equivalence class of DAGs: an edge stays undirected exactly when its orientation varies across the class. It is what constraint-based causal discovery algorithms such as PC estimate from observational data, and dag_to_cpdag() computes it from a DAG.
An MPDAG is a CPDAG with background knowledge added, which may orient edges the equivalence class alone leaves undetermined.


plot(dag_to_cpdag(dag))








See Equivalence Classes for worked examples of all three.


Acyclic directed mixed graphs
An ADMG (acyclic directed mixed graph) has directed (-->) and bidirected (<->) edges. Directed edges are causal relations, while a bidirected edge is unobserved confounding between its endpoints. An ADMG is, for example, what latent_project() gives when it projects latent variables out of a DAG:

full <- cgraph(U %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y)
plot(latent_project(full, "U"))










Ancestral graphs
Ancestral graphs ("AG" and its maximal subclass "MAG") have directed (-->), bidirected (<->) and undirected (---) edges. In an ancestral graph, an arrowhead at a node means that node is not an ancestor of the other endpoint. A bidirected edge thus means neither endpoint is an ancestor of the other; in causal applications such edges commonly represent unobserved confounding.
Undirected edges mean something different here than in a PDAG: rather than an unknown orientation, they represent selection bias, associations arising from conditioning on variables that are common effects. A MAG is the ancestral graph of a DAG with latent and selection variables marginalized and conditioned out, and is maximal: every pair of non-adjacent nodes can be separated.


Partial ancestral graphs
A PAG plays the role for MAGs that a CPDAG plays for DAGs: it represents a Markov equivalence class of MAGs (Zhang 2008), and is what the FCI algorithm estimates. PAG edges can have three endpoint marks: a tail, an arrowhead or a circle, and a circle means that mark is not the same in every MAG in the class. mag_to_pag() computes the PAG of a MAG:

mag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, C %-->% B, B %-->% D, class = "MAG")
plot(mag_to_pag(mag))








See PAG Causal Effects for estimating causal effects from a PAG.


Undirected graphs
A UG ("UG") has only undirected (---) edges. Undirected graphs are not common in causal inference, but are available for those who need them; for example, moralize() returns one.


Unknown graphs
"UNKNOWN" imposes no structural constraints. It accepts every edge type, including self-loops and parallel edges, for graphs that do not fit any other class:

edges(cgraph(A %-->% B, A %<->% B, B %-->% B, class = "UNKNOWN"))
#>   from to type
#> 1    A  B  -->
#> 2    A  B  <->
#> 3    B  B  -->

title: Graph Classes
text:
Background knowledge
Sometimes you know some causal relations in advance: A must cause B, or C does not cause D. apply_background_knowledge() adds such knowledge to a PDAG, required edges as %-->% (or %<--%) and forbidden ones as %!-->% (or %!<--%), and propagates the orientations it implies, giving an MPDAG:

cpdag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C, class = "CPDAG")
plot(apply_background_knowledge(cpdag, A %-->% B))








dag_to_mpdag() does the same starting from a DAG, using its CPDAG.

title: Benchmarks
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/benchmarks.qmd
Every graph in CausalStructures precomputes and stores each node’s parents, children, spouses, and neighbors directly, so parents(), children(), spouses(), and neighbors() are effectively \(O(1)\) lookups rather than scans over the whole edge set. Many higher-level algorithms, including d_separated()/m_separated(), minimal_separator(), and adjustment-set search, are built on these primitive operations, so their performance depends directly on the efficiency of these basic queries.
library(CausalStructures)

# The median time of each expression. Memory allocated inside the library, and
# its garbage collection, is invisible to bench, so only the time is shown.
timings <- function(..., iterations = 200) {
  b <- bench::mark(..., iterations = iterations, check = FALSE)
  data.frame(expression = names(b$expression), median = format(b$median))
}

title: Benchmarks
section: Queries stay fast as graphs grow
text:
Queries stay fast as graphs grow
Single-hop queries such as children() are just slice lookups, so their runtime is essentially unchanged whether the graph has 100 nodes or 10,000:

graphs <- lapply(c(100, 1000, 10000), \(n) {
  generate_graph(n, p = 5 / n, seed = 1)
})
timings(
  "n = 100" = children(graphs[[1]], "V50"),
  "n = 1,000" = children(graphs[[2]], "V500"),
  "n = 10,000" = children(graphs[[3]], "V5000")
)
#>   expression median
#> 1    n = 100 1.63µs
#> 2  n = 1,000 1.64µs
#> 3 n = 10,000 1.65µs

These primitives keep more involved queries fast too, on graphs with hundreds of nodes and across graph classes:

dag <- generate_graph(500, p = 0.1, seed = 1)
mag <- generate_graph(500, p = 0.01, class = "MAG", latents = 20, seed = 1)
x <- "V10"
y <- "V290"

timings(
  "d_separated (DAG)" = d_separated(dag, x, y),
  "m_separated (MAG)" = m_separated(mag, x, y),
  "topological_sort" = topological_sort(dag),
  "minimal_separator" = minimal_separator(dag, x, y),
  "markov_blanket" = markov_blanket(dag, x)
)
#>          expression  median
#> 1 d_separated (DAG) 135.8µs
#> 2 m_separated (MAG)  12.9µs
#> 3  topological_sort  55.7µs
#> 4 minimal_separator 157.7µs
#> 5    markov_blanket  15.1µs

title: Benchmarks
text:
Searching for adjustment sets
all_backdoor_sets(), all_adjustment_sets(), all_iv_sets(), and all_frontdoor_sets() search subsets of the candidate universe up to max_size, checking each one against the relevant validity criterion. Consequently, the runtime grows exponentially with max_size:

admg <- generate_graph(35, p = 0.15, class = "ADMG", latents = 8, seed = 1)
x <- "V3"
y <- "V33"

sizes <- 2:4
n_sets <- vapply(
  sizes,
  \(ms) length(all_adjustment_sets(admg, x, y, minimal = FALSE, max_size = ms)),
  integer(1)
)
cbind(
  timings(
    "max_size = 2" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 2
    ),
    "max_size = 3" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 3
    ),
    "max_size = 4" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 4
    ),
    iterations = 20
  ),
  sets = n_sets
)
#>     expression   median sets
#> 1 max_size = 2   1.46ms   33
#> 2 max_size = 3  18.13ms  272
#> 3 max_size = 4 152.13ms 1537

title: Benchmarks
text:
Expensive algorithms
Here we will show the performance of some of the most expensive algorithms.

Exact uniform DAG sampling
generate_graph() uses an Erdős–Rényi model: it samples each edge independently, which is cheap regardless of n but is not uniform over the space of DAGs. uniform_dag() instead draws exactly uniformly from all labeled DAGs on n nodes using the recursive enumeration algorithm of Kuipers and Moffa (2015):1

timings(
  "n = 10" = uniform_dag(10, seed = 1),
  "n = 20" = uniform_dag(20, seed = 1),
  "n = 40" = uniform_dag(40, seed = 1),
  iterations = 20
)
#>   expression   median
#> 1     n = 10  94.17µs
#> 2     n = 20 645.96µs
#> 3     n = 40   5.69ms



Markov equivalence class enumeration
count_dags() and enumerate_dags() operate on a CPDAG, PDAG, or MPDAG by considering every DAG in its Markov equivalence class. The size of that class grows combinatorially with the number of undirected edges. For example, a clique on \(k\) nodes has \(k!\) consistent orientations, so the class can grow very large very quickly:

# A PDAG whose k nodes are all joined by undirected edges
clique <- function(k) {
  pairs <- utils::combn(paste0("V", seq_len(k)), 2)
  cgraph(
    spec = paste(pairs[1, ], "---", pairs[2, ], collapse = ", "),
    class = "PDAG"
  )
}
cliques <- lapply(c(5, 7, 8), clique)
vapply(cliques, count_dags, numeric(1))
#> [1]   120  5040 40320

timings(
  "count_dags, k = 5" = count_dags(cliques[[1]]),
  "count_dags, k = 7" = count_dags(cliques[[2]]),
  "count_dags, k = 8" = count_dags(cliques[[3]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 5" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[1]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 7" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[2]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 8" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[3]]),
  iterations = 5
)
#>              expression  median
#> 1     count_dags, k = 5 488.9µs
#> 2     count_dags, k = 7    35ms
#> 3     count_dags, k = 8 273.8ms
#> 4 enumerate_dags, k = 5   569µs
#> 5 enumerate_dags, k = 7  38.4ms
#> 6 enumerate_dags, k = 8 446.4ms

enumerate_dags() must materialize every DAG rather than simply count them, so it is slower and uses more memory than count_dags(), as the numbers above show. In R, every DAG it returns is also a cgraph, so keep the class small, or use count_dags() first to check its size.


MAG equivalence class enumeration
enumerate_mags() is the PAG/MAG counterpart to enumerate_dags(). While enumerate_dags() is fairly efficient via Chickering’s recursive pruning, enumerate_mags() simply brute-forces every tail/arrowhead assignment for each circle endpoint in the PAG (\(2^k\) candidates for \(k\) circle endpoints), and keeps the candidates that are valid MAGs with the given PAG as their equivalence class. Thus, it’s considerably more expensive than count_dags()/enumerate_dags():

# A PAG whose k nodes are all joined by o-o edges
circle_clique <- function(k) {
  pairs <- utils::combn(paste0("V", seq_len(k)), 2)
  cgraph(
    spec = paste(pairs[1, ], "o-o", pairs[2, ], collapse = ", "),
    class = "PAG"
  )
}
pags <- lapply(3:4, circle_clique)
vapply(pags, \(pag) length(enumerate_mags(pag)), integer(1))
#> [1]  23 242

timings(
  "k = 3" = enumerate_mags(pags[[1]]),
  "k = 4" = enumerate_mags(pags[[2]]),
  iterations = 5
)
#>   expression   median
#> 1      k = 3   3.26ms
#> 2      k = 4    302ms

With one more node, k = 5, the class has 4,457 MAGs among \(2^{20}\) candidates, and enumerate_mags() takes tens of seconds.






TipParallel search



count_dags(), enumerate_dags(), enumerate_mags(), pagcauses(), and the whole all_*_sets() family2 parallelize their search across the library’s threads automatically once the problem is large enough to benefit. The library runs with one thread unless the JULIA_NUM_THREADS environment variable (a number, or "auto" for one per core) is set before the package is loaded, e.g. in your .Renviron.

title: Equivalence Classes
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/equivalence-classes.qmd
Equivalence classes of graphs arise in several settings, for instance, during causal discovery algorithms. This guide covers the graph classes that represent such classes and how to work with them.
library(CausalStructures)

title: Equivalence Classes
text:
Equivalence classes of DAGs
A PDAG (partially directed acyclic graph) is a graph whose edges may be directed or undirected, with no directed cycles. Two DAGs are Markov equivalent if and only if they have the same skeleton and the same v-structures (unshielded colliders).
Each Markov equivalence class of DAGs has a unique CPDAG (completed partially directed acyclic graph) representation. In a CPDAG, an edge is directed precisely when it has the same orientation in every DAG in the equivalence class; otherwise it remains undirected.
Given a DAG, dag_to_cpdag() computes its CPDAG:

dag <- cgraph(C %-->% X, A %-->% X + Y, Y %-->% Z)
cpdag <- dag_to_cpdag(dag)
plot(cpdag)








The v-structure C --> X <-- A appears in every DAG in the equivalence class and therefore remains directed. The edges A --- Y and Y --- Z are undirected because no v-structure or Meek rule forces their orientation.
count_dags() tells us how many DAGs are in the class, and enumerate_dags() lists them all:

count_dags(cpdag)
#> [1] 3


enumerate_dags(cpdag)
#> [[1]]
#> DAG with 5 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, C, X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     A --> X, C --> X, A --> Y, Y --> Z
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> DAG with 5 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, C, X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     Y --> A, A --> X, C --> X, Y --> Z
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> DAG with 5 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, C, X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     Y --> A, A --> X, C --> X, Z --> Y

When you need one concrete DAG to work with, dag_from_pdag() picks one:

dag_from_pdag(cpdag)
#> DAG with 5 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, C, X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     C --> X, A --> X, A --> Y, Y --> Z

You can compute adjustment sets on a CPDAG, and the result is valid for every DAG in the equivalence class:

all_adjustment_sets(cpdag, "X", "Z")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "A"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "Y"

An MPDAG (maximally oriented partially directed acyclic graph) can, for instance, arise when background knowledge is incorporated during causal discovery, orienting some edges of a CPDAG.
meek_closure() propagates all further orientations implied by Meek’s rules on a PDAG to obtain an MPDAG:

pdag <- cgraph(C %---% X, A %-->% X, A %---% Y, Y %-->% Z, class = "PDAG")
mpdag <- meek_closure(pdag)
mpdag
#> MPDAG with 5 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, C, X, Y, Z
#>   edges:
#>     A --- Y, X --> C, A --> X, Y --> Z

Here, X --- C was oriented to X --> C using Meek’s rules.
All the functions shown above work on any PDAG, CPDAG or MPDAG:

count_dags(pdag)
#> [1] 2
all_adjustment_sets(mpdag, "X", "Z")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "A"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "Y"







NoteOnly CPDAGs are guaranteed to be extendable



Every CPDAG represents a non-empty Markov equivalence class, so it always admits at least one consistent DAG extension and dag_from_pdag() is guaranteed to succeed. This is not true for a general PDAG or MPDAG: being acyclic (and, for an MPDAG, closed under Meek’s rules) is not sufficient to ensure a consistent extension exists. For example, a chordless undirected cycle is a valid PDAG and MPDAG, yet it cannot be oriented into a DAG without introducing a new v-structure:

cg <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C %---% D %---% A, class = "PDAG")
is_cpdag(cg)
#> [1] FALSE
is_mpdag(cg)
#> [1] TRUE
dag_from_pdag(cg)
#> Error:
#> ! PDAG cannot be extended to a DAG (Dor-Tarsi failed)

title: Equivalence Classes
text:
Equivalence classes of MAGs
Maximal ancestral graphs (MAGs) naturally arise when some common causes are unobserved: every latent common cause between two observed nodes becomes a bidirected edge (<->) in the MAG. Two MAGs are Markov equivalent if they encode the same conditional independence structure over the observed variables.
Each Markov equivalence class of MAGs has a unique PAG (partial ancestral graph). Like a CPDAG for DAGs, the PAG marks each endpoint with the symbol shared by every MAG in the class. A circle (o) at an endpoint means that mark is not invariant; some MAGs in the class have a tail there and others have an arrowhead.
Consider a MAG where A and B share a hidden common cause, C directly causes B, and B directly causes D:

mag <- cgraph(A %<->% B, C %-->% B %-->% D, class = "MAG")
mag
#> MAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A <-> B, C --> B, B --> D

mag_to_pag() computes the PAG representing the Markov equivalence class of this MAG, so all MAGs that encode the same conditional independences:

pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
pag
#> PAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A o-> B, C o-> B, B --> D

The arrowheads at B on the A-B and C-B edges are invariant: A, B, and C form an unshielded collider at B (since A and C are non-adjacent), so every MAG in the class has an edge pointing into B from both sides. The circle marks at A and C are not invariant; the A-B edge could be A --> B or A <-> B, and similarly for C. The B --> D edge is invariant via Zhang’s orientation rule R1: since A and D are non-adjacent and A o-> B --> D, the tail at B is forced in all MAGs.
enumerate_mags() lets you explore the equivalence class:

enumerate_mags(pag)
#> [[1]]
#> MAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, C --> B, B --> D
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> MAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A <-> B, C --> B, B --> D
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> MAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, B <-> C, B --> D
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> MAG with 4 nodes and 3 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C, D
#>   edges:
#>     A <-> B, B <-> C, B --> D

You can also answer various causal inference questions, see PAG Causal Effects for some examples.

text: Source: R/transform.R

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Description
Orients cg according to background knowledge about direct causes: required edges (A %-->% B, A must directly cause B) and forbidden ones (A %!-->% B, A must not).

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Usage
apply_background_knowledge(cg, ..., spec = NULL)

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Arguments



cg


A PDAG-family graph (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) created with cgraph().




...


Required (%-->%, %<--%) and forbidden (%!-->%, %!<--%) edges; see edge-operators. Mutually exclusive with spec.




spec


Background knowledge as a string, e.g. "A --> B, C !--> D", for programmatic use. Mutually exclusive with ....

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Details
Requiring A --> B orients A --- B that way, and forbidding it orients A --- B as B --> A; after each, Meek’s rules propagate the orientations it implies. Background knowledge only orients edges, so it errors when it would add or remove one: a required edge between non-adjacent nodes or against an orientation cg (or an earlier item) already has, or a forbidden edge cg already has.

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Value
A cgraph of class MPDAG.

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
References
Meek C (1995). “Causal inference and causal explanation with background knowledge.” In Proceedings of UAI 1995, 403–410.

title: Apply background knowledge to a PDAG
text:
Examples

cpdag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C, class = "CPDAG")
apply_background_knowledge(cpdag, A %-->% B)
#> MPDAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, B --> C
apply_background_knowledge(cpdag, C %!-->% B)
#> MPDAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     A --- B, B --> C

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text: Source: R/metrics.R

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Description
Counts the ordered pairs of distinct nodes (t, y) for which cg_test leads to a wrong conclusion about the causal effect of t on y relative to cg_truth. For each pair, an adjustment set is read off cg_test with the strategy type, and it is a mistake if that set is not a valid adjustment set in cg_truth.

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Usage
aid(
  cg_truth,
  cg_test,
  type = c("oset", "parent", "ancestor"),
  normalized = FALSE
)

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Arguments



cg_truth


The ground-truth graph: a DAG or PDAG-family graph (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG) created with cgraph().




cg_test


The graph to evaluate, of the same kinds and with the same nodes as cg_truth.




type


The adjustment strategy: "oset" (default; the optimal adjustment set, see adjustment_set()), "parent" (the parents of t), or "ancestor" (the ancestors of t, which makes the distance zero whenever cg_test respects the causal order of cg_truth).




normalized


If TRUE, divide by the number of ordered pairs, n * (n - 1), giving a value in [0, 1].

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Details
Outside the pairs its adjustment set applies to (y not a possible descendant of t in cg_test, or, for "parent", y a parent of t), the strategy instead claims a zero effect, which is correct if y is not a possible descendant of t in cg_truth. For a PDAG-family cg_test where the effect is not identifiable, the strategy claims so, which is correct if it is not identifiable in cg_truth either.
To compare causal discovery algorithms against a known true graph, first convert the truth to the class the algorithms estimate: dag_to_cpdag() for algorithms returning a CPDAG (such as PC). Otherwise edges the algorithm correctly leaves unoriented count as mistakes. If an estimate is an MPDAG built from background knowledge, apply the same knowledge to the true CPDAG with apply_background_knowledge().

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Value
A number: the count of mistaken pairs, or its share of all ordered pairs if normalized = TRUE.

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
References
Henckel L, Würtzen T, Weichwald S (2024). “Adjustment Identification Distance: A gadjid for Causal Structure Learning.” In Proceedings of the Fortieth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, volume 244 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research.

title: Adjustment Identification Distance
text:
Examples

truth <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C, A %-->% C)
guess <- cgraph(A %-->% B %-->% C)
aid(truth, guess)
#> [1] 1
aid(truth, guess, type = "parent")
#> [1] 1
aid(truth, guess, type = "ancestor")
#> [1] 0

title: Node-set queries
text:
Description
parents() and children() are the nodes directly connected to node by a directed edge. ancestors() and descendants() are all nodes from which (respectively, to which) node is reachable by following directed edges. spouses() are the nodes connected to node by a bidirected edge (node <-> spouse).

text:

children(cg, node)

spouses(cg, node)

text:
Arguments



cg


A graph created with cgraph(). Supported classes vary by function:


parents(), children(): any class except UG.


ancestors(), descendants(): DAG, PDAG-family (PDAG, CPDAG, MPDAG), ADMG, or AG-family (AG, MAG).


spouses(): ADMG, AG-family (AG, MAG), or PAG.






node


Node name.




open

text:

title: Node-set queries

#> [1] "X"

#> [1] "M"
ancestors(dag, "Y")
#> [1] "A" "M" "X"
descendants(dag, "X")

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
Description
Finds an instrument z for the causal effect of x on y, together with a conditioning set given that makes it valid (see is_valid_iv()). For each candidate instrument, given is a separator of y and the instrument in the graph with the first edge of every causal path from x to y removed, chosen nearest to y. The pair with the smallest given is returned, so an unconditional instrument is preferred.

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
Usage
iv_set(cg, x, y, restrict = NULL)

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph().




x


Exposure node name.




y


Outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




restrict


Character vector of the nodes allowed in z and given, e.g. the observed ones. NULL (default) allows every node.

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
Value
A list with character vectors z and given, or NULL if no instrument exists.

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
References
van der Zander B, Textor J, Liśkiewicz M (2015). “Efficiently Finding Conditional Instruments for Causal Inference.” In Proceedings of the 24th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2015), 3243–3249.

title: Find an instrument and its conditioning set
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(W %-->% Z + Y, Z %-->% X %-->% Y, U %-->% X + Y)
iv_set(dag, "X", "Y")
#> $z
#> [1] "Z"
#> 
#> $given
#> [1] "W"

# Without W observed, there is no instrument
is.null(iv_set(dag, "X", "Y", restrict = c("Z", "X", "Y")))
#> [1] TRUE

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text: Source: R/identification.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Description
cg (a PDAG, CPDAG, or MPDAG) represents a Markov equivalence class (MEC) of DAGs. enumerate_dags() lists every DAG in that class; count_dags() counts them without materializing them, which is much cheaper and useful for sizing the problem before calling enumerate_dags(), since a MEC can be very large.

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Usage
count_dags(cg)

enumerate_dags(cg)

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Arguments



cg


A PDAG, CPDAG, or MPDAG created with cgraph().

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Details
Both apply Meek closure to cg first to normalize it, then branch on each undirected edge in lexicographic order, rejecting orientations that would introduce a new v-structure or a directed cycle, and propagating forced orientations via Meek’s rules at each step (Chickering’s (2002) recursive listing algorithm).

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Value
For count_dags(), the number of DAGs (a double if it is too large for an integer). For enumerate_dags(), a list of cgraphs of class DAG. If cg has no consistent DAG extension, 0 and an empty list.

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
References
Chickering DM (2002). “Learning Equivalence Classes of Bayesian-Network Structures.” Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2, 445–498.

title: Count and enumerate DAGs in a Markov equivalence class
text:
Examples

pdag <- cgraph(A %---% B, B %---% C, class = "PDAG")
count_dags(pdag)
#> [1] 3

pdag <- cgraph(A %---% B, B %---% C, class = "PDAG")
enumerate_dags(pdag)
#> [[1]]
#> DAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, B --> C
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> DAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     B --> A, B --> C
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> DAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     B --> A, C --> B

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
Description
Returns a set Z, containing include and contained in restrict, satisfying all three front-door conditions (Algorithm 1 of the reference below) for the causal effect of x on y. Validate a candidate set directly with is_valid_frontdoor().

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
Usage
frontdoor_set(cg, x, y, include = character(), restrict = NULL)

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph(). For an ADMG, the backdoor and condition-3 checks use m-separation, with bidirected edges treated as latent-confounder edges (a spouse contributes an arrowhead into a node just like a directed parent does).




x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




include


Character vector of nodes forced into the set.




restrict


Character vector of candidate nodes the set is drawn from. NULL (default) allows every node except x and y.

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
Value
Character vector with a valid frontdoor set, or NULL if none exists.

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
References
Jeong H, Tian J, Bareinboim E (2022). “Finding and Listing Front-door Adjustment Sets.” In Koyejo S, Mohamed S, Agarwal A, Belgrave D, Cho K, Oh A (eds.), Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, volume 35, 33173–33185. https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/d67ac621411d6fa4dca682ce62f84ea7-Paper-Conference.pdf.

title: Find a frontdoor adjustment set
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(U %-->% X, U %-->% Y, X %-->% Z, Z %-->% Y)
frontdoor_set(dag, "X", "Y") # Z mediates X -> Y
#> [1] "Z"
frontdoor_set(dag, "X", "Y", restrict = "Z")
#> [1] "Z"

title: Validate a backdoor adjustment set
text:
Description
Tests whether given is a valid backdoor set for the effect of x on y. It is if (1) no node in given is a descendant of x, and (2) given blocks every backdoor path from x to y (every parent of x is d-separated from y given given together with x).

text:

title: Validate a backdoor adjustment set
text:

A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph().




x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




given

title: Validate a backdoor adjustment set
text:

TRUE if given satisfies the backdoor criterion.

title: Validate a backdoor adjustment set
text:

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% X, X %-->% Y, A %-->% Y)
is_valid_backdoor(dag, "X", "Y") # A --> Y left open
#> [1] FALSE
is_valid_backdoor(dag, "X", "Y", "A")
#> [1] TRUE

title: Validate a frontdoor criterion set
text:
Description
Tests whether given is a valid front-door set for the effect of x on y. It is if (1) it intercepts every directed path from x to y, (2) there is no unblocked backdoor path from x to any node in given, and (3) for every node in given, all backdoor paths to y are blocked by x together with the rest of given. When these hold, the effect is identified via the front-door formula even with unmeasured confounders between x and y.

text:
Usage
is_valid_frontdoor(cg, x, y, given = character())

title: Validate a frontdoor criterion set
text:
Arguments



cg


A DAG or ADMG created with cgraph().




x, y


Exposure and outcome node name, or character vector of node names.




given


Character vector of conditioning node names (may be empty).

title: Validate a frontdoor criterion set
text:
Value
TRUE if the configuration satisfies the frontdoor criterion.

title: Validate a frontdoor criterion set
text:
Examples

dag <- cgraph(U %-->% X, X %-->% M, M %-->% Y, U %-->% Y)
is_valid_frontdoor(dag, "X", "Y", "M")
#> [1] TRUE
is_valid_frontdoor(dag, "X", "Y") # X -> M -> Y left open
#> [1] FALSE

text:

Builds a graph from edge expressions using the operators documented at edge-operators, e.g. A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y. A bare node name (or +-combination of names) declares isolated node(s).

title: Create a causal graph
Create a causal graph
text:
Arguments



...


Edge expressions (see edge-operators) and/or bare node declarations. Mutually exclusive with spec.




spec


Graph specification string, for programmatic construction. Mutually exclusive with ....




class


Graph class: "DAG", "UG", "PDAG", "CPDAG", "MPDAG", "ADMG", "AG", "MAG", "PAG", or "UNKNOWN" (no structural constraints; accepts all edge types, including multiple edges between the same pair of nodes).

Details
For programmatic construction (e.g. from an edge list assembled at runtime), pass a spec string directly via spec instead of ..., using the same syntax as the operators expand to (e.g. "A --> X + Y, X --> M --> Y").

A cgraph: a reference to a graph held by the Julia library. It can be saved and loaded like any R object (e.g. with saveRDS()).

dag <- cgraph(A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y, class = "DAG")
cpdag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C, class = "CPDAG")

# equivalent to the dag above, built from a spec string
dag2 <- cgraph(spec = "A --> X + Y, X --> M --> Y", class = "DAG")

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Description
Returns every valid adjustment set relative to (x, y) in some MAG consistent with the PAG cg, i.e. the possible causal effects of x on y identifiable via covariate adjustment. It does so without enumerating MAGs (PAGcauses, Algorithm 1).

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Usage
pagcauses(cg, x, y)

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Arguments



cg


A PAG created with cgraph().




x, y


Exposure and outcome node names.

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Details
If x is not a possible ancestor of y, returns an empty list (no causal effect). If the causal effect is already identifiable directly in cg (backdoor_set()), returns that single set. Otherwise, this searches every valid local structure at x (possible_local_structures()) and its maximal local MAG (maximal_local_mag()) for potential adjustment sets.
Assumes cg has no selection bias (no undirected edges).

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Value
List of character vectors (empty list if x has no possible causal effect on y).

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
References
Wang T, Tao L, Qin T, Zhou Z (2025). “Estimating possible causal effects with latent variables via adjustment and novel rule orientation.” Artificial Intelligence, 347, 104387.

title: Find every possible causal effect in a PAG (PAGcauses)
text:
Examples

pag <- cgraph(
  X %o->% Y, X %o->% C, X %o->% A, Y %o-o% C, C %o-o% A,
  B %o->% C, B %o->% Y, B %o->% A,
  class = "PAG"
)
pagcauses(pag, "X", "Y")
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "A" "B"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "C"
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> [1] "B" "C"
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> [1] "A" "B" "C"

text: Source: R/transform.R, R/jlbind-wrappers.R

title: Convert an AG to a Markov equivalent MAG
text:
Description
Adds an edge between every pair of non-adjacent nodes in the AG cg that cannot be m-separated by any subset of the remaining nodes, producing a Markov equivalent MAG.

title: Convert an AG to a Markov equivalent MAG
text:
Usage
ag_to_mag(cg)

Arguments



cg


An AG created with cgraph().

title: Convert an AG to a Markov equivalent MAG
text:
Details
For each such pair (u, v), the edge is directed toward whichever node is not an ancestor of the other, or bidirected if neither is an ancestor of the other. Edges are added one at a time, with the graph re-evaluated after each addition (a new edge can change m-separation and ancestor relationships).

title: Convert an AG to a Markov equivalent MAG
text:
Value
A cgraph of class MAG.

title: Convert an AG to a Markov equivalent MAG
text:
Examples

ag <- cgraph(A %-->% B, B %-->% C, class = "AG")
ag_to_mag(ag)
#> MAG with 3 nodes and 2 edges:
#>   nodes: A, B, C
#>   edges:
#>     A --> B, B --> C

title: CausalStructures
text:
CausalStructures is an R binding to the Julia package CausalStructures.jl, for representing, validating, and reasoning about causal graphs


Install CausalStructures from GitHub:
pak::pak("BjarkeHautop/CausalStructures")
CausalStructures needs Julia (>= 1.13); see https://julialang.org/install/ for the recommended way to install Julia. Once the package is installed, build the compiled CausalStructures.jl library it calls with
jlbind::install_library()
This takes a few minutes while Julia downloads and compiles the dependencies, and needs to be redone after installing or updating CausalStructures (or any other package built on jlbind, since they share one compiled library). Pass julia = "/path/to/julia" (or set the JULIA environment variable) to use a Julia other than the one on the PATH.
The compiled library uses the runtime of the Julia that built it, so run jlbind::install_library(force = TRUE) again if that Julia is removed (for example by a juliaup update).



The following graph types are supported, shown here following the abstract type hierarchy from CausalStructures.jl:
CausalGraph
├─ DAG            Directed Acyclic Graph
├─ UG             Undirected Graph
├─ AbstractPDAG   All Partially Directed Acyclic Graphs
│  ├─ PDAG        Partially Directed Acyclic Graph
│  ├─ CPDAG       Completed Partially Directed Acyclic Graph
│  └─ MPDAG       Maximally Oriented Partially Directed Acyclic Graph
├─ ADMG           Acyclic Directed Mixed Graph
├─ AbstractAG     All Ancestral Graphs
│  ├─ AG          Ancestral Graph
│  └─ MAG         Maximal Ancestral Graph
├─ PAG            Partial Ancestral Graph
└─ UNKNOWN        No structural constraints
Each graph class encodes structural constraints, such as no cycles, closed under Meek’s rules, etc., and these constraints are verified on construction.



First, we define a causal graph using the cgraph() function, giving its edges and its class:
library(CausalStructures)

dag <- cgraph("A --> X + Y, X --> M --> Y", class = "DAG")

# Alternatively, wrap the edges in %...%, and then not use a string:
cgraph(A %-->% X + Y, X %-->% M %-->% Y, class = "DAG")
#> DAG with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, M, X, Y
#>   edges:
#>     A --> X, A --> Y, X --> M, M --> Y
You can then run a number of queries and transformations on the causal graph:
parents(dag, "Y")
#> [1] "A" "M"
adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y")
#> [1] "A"

cpdag <- dag_to_cpdag(dag)
cpdag
#> CPDAG with 4 nodes and 4 edges:
#>   nodes: A, M, X, Y
#>   edges:
#>     A --- X, M --- X, M --> Y, A --> Y
and plot it, here highlighting the treatment, the outcome and the adjustment set:
cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightskyblue", nodes = c("X", "Y")) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "gold", nodes = adjustment_set(dag, "X", "Y"))




The DAG drawn left to right, with X and Y in blue and the adjustment set, A, in gold.


See the documentation site for the full documentation.



Some algorithms (all_backdoor_sets(), all_adjustment_sets(), all_frontdoor_sets(), enumerate_dags(), count_dags(), enumerate_mags(), pagcauses()) can use multiple threads. To do so, set the JULIA_NUM_THREADS environment variable (a number, or "auto" for one per core) before loading the package, for example in your .Renviron file or with
Sys.setenv(JULIA_NUM_THREADS = "4")
library(CausalStructures)
